assertion: The Saint Paul protection arrangement originated under Police Chief John O'Connor in 1900.
locators: S01, opening narrative
supportExplanation: Minnesota Historical Society accounts document O'Connor instituting the system at the start of his tenure.
qualification: Predates national Prohibition; informal policy rather than formal municipal legislation.

assertion: Check-in, regular payments, and restraint from major crimes inside Saint Paul were the core conditions of refuge.
locators: S01, conditions paragraph
supportExplanation: Described in historical accounts as the three pillars of the O'Connor layover agreement.
qualification: The examined historical accounts describe an informal system; this project has not examined a signed agreement.

assertion: William 'Reddy' Griffin preceded Dan Hogan as the chief intermediary between criminals and police.
locators: S01, succession paragraphs
supportExplanation: MNHS account identifies Griffin as the initial broker until his death in 1913.
qualification: Do not collapse all earlier activity into Hogan's later saloon venue.

assertion: The Green Lantern Saloon on Wabasha Street was associated with Dan Hogan and criminal gatherings.
locators: S02, Green Lantern paragraph
supportExplanation: Historical accounts document the saloon as Hogan's operational base and a prominent underworld meeting place.
qualification: Association with a gathering place does not locate every transaction there.

assertion: Chief O'Connor retired in 1920; Dan Hogan was assassinated in a car bombing in 1928.
locators: S01, later narrative
supportExplanation: Documents O'Connor's retirement and Hogan's violent death.
qualification: The MNHS account describes the bombing as unsolved.

assertion: The 18th Amendment was ratified in 1919 taking effect in 1920; the 21st Amendment repealed it on December 5, 1933.
locators: S13, Amendments XVIII and XXI annotations
supportExplanation: Official constitutional records of ratification and repeal dates.
qualification: Constitutional prohibition differs from the statutory Volstead Act; June 1933 preceded repeal.

assertion: Hotel history associates Leon Gleckman's headquarters and Treasury agent Malone's surveillance with the Saint Paul Hotel.
supportExplanation: Institutional retrospective records the suite association and surveillance.
qualification: Institutional account; no specific permanent suite number or staff complicity established.

assertion: Federal tax prosecution of Gleckman required distinguishing gross bank deposits from net taxable income.
supportExplanation: Appellate court held that bank deposits alone do not constitute taxable income without eliminating loans and capital.
qualification: Reflects the specific appellate holding in that proceeding.

assertion: Gleckman's federal tax convictions were affirmed for 1929 and 1930, while he was acquitted on the 1931 count.
locators: S04, 80 F.2d 394, p. 400 and disposition
supportExplanation: Eighth Circuit formal disposition affirmed convictions on counts 1 and 2, noting acquittal on count 3.
qualification: Preserve the partial acquittal; do not misrepresent as conviction on all counts.

assertion: Gleckman's criminal contempt convictions for jury tampering were affirmed on appeal in 1938.
supportExplanation: Appellate record details payments and credit extended to juror Fuchs following a 1934 mistrial.
qualification: Adjudicated under criminal contempt rather than a separate statutory bribery indictment.

assertion: Gleckman and first trial jurors lodged at the Saint Paul Hotel during proceedings.
supportExplanation: Contempt opinion records physical proximity of defendant and jurors at the hotel.
qualification: Proximity is not proof of hotel management complicity.

assertion: Castle Royal, Inc. corporate notice was published in Commercial West on September 30, 1933.
locators: S06, Commercial West, Sept 30, 1933, p. 19
supportExplanation: Contemporaneous corporate incorporation notice in financial press.
qualification: A period business announcement, not the original incorporation filing; it does not establish patrons or an opening date.

assertion: Historian Greg Brick dates Castle Royal nightclub opening to October 26, 1933.
supportExplanation: Scholarly study of Twin Cities subterranean venues provides opening date.
qualification: Attributed to Brick's historical monograph.

assertion: Famous gangsters such as John Dillinger or Ma Barker frequented Castle Royal as patrons.
locators: S07, p. 115; S15 tourism listing
supportExplanation: Brick discusses conflicting later recollections and reports the lack of proof for named gangster attendance.
qualification: Disputed or unverified in the examined material. Later recollections do not establish when the stories originated.

assertion: William Hamm Jr. was kidnapped on June 15, 1933, held for $100,000 ransom, and released alive.
locators: S08, p. 13; S09 Hamm narrative
supportExplanation: Both local historical society and FBI records confirm abduction, ransom, and release.
qualification: Released alive. The sources do not justify treating that outcome as absence of harm.

assertion: Historical accounts associate William Hamm Jr.'s abduction point with 671 Cable Street (later Greenbrier).
locators: S08, p. 13; S02 photograph caption
supportExplanation: Ramsey County History documents the residence location as the abduction site.
qualification: The RCHS account identifies a former residence; the FBI retrospective describes Hamm leaving his office. The precise abduction footprint is unresolved in this project.

assertion: FBI investigators visualized latent fingerprints on Hamm ransom letters using silver nitrate.
locators: S09, Hamm investigation
supportExplanation: FBI case history credits silver nitrate development with establishing Barker-Karpis culpability.
qualification: Institutional agency account; not an assertion of being the first in all world forensic history.

assertion: Edward Bremer was kidnapped on January 17, 1934 at Lexington and Goodrich after dropping his daughter at school.
locators: S10, printed p. 18 / PDF p. 19
supportExplanation: Federal investigative summary documents exact date, location, and circumstances.
qualification: Date is January 17, 1934; corrects printing error in S08.

assertion: Investigators reported Harry Sawyer advocated kidnapping Bremer over robbing Commercial State Bank for larger returns.
locators: S10, printed p. 17; confirm PDF viewer offset against the printed folio before quotation.
supportExplanation: Federal summary records Sawyer's calculation of expected extortion yield.
qualification: Attributed to post-arrest investigative reports, not a wiretap transcript.

assertion: Bremer kidnappers demanded $200,000 ransom and coerced Walter Magee under threats of violence against police contact.
locators: S10, printed pp. 18–19 / PDF pp. 19–20
supportExplanation: Federal summary documents ransom letters and coercive threats against reporting.
qualification: Threats were coercive tactics; captor promises were not factual findings.

assertion: Local and federal authorities were notified immediately by Walter Magee and the Bremer family upon receipt of threats.
locators: S10, printed p. 19 / PDF p. 20
supportExplanation: Investigation summary confirms law enforcement was engaged despite extortionists' warnings.
qualification: Captor demands for secrecy did not produce compliance.

assertion: Edward Bremer was released by his captors after approximately three weeks of captivity following ransom payment.
locators: S09, Bremer section
supportExplanation: Agency case overview confirms duration of captivity and release in Wisconsin.
qualification: Rounded duration; exact daily release log not essential to tour.

assertion: Interstate transportation of a stolen car under the Dyer Act provided federal jurisdiction to hunt Dillinger.
locators: S11, 'The Bureau Actively Joins the Hunt'
supportExplanation: FBI history details how crossing state lines with the Lake County sheriff's vehicle triggered federal authority.
qualification: This specific jurisdictional development does not imply that federal officers could never previously assist.

assertion: Manager report on March 30, 1934 led to the March 31 shootout and Dillinger's escape at Lincoln Court.
locators: S11, Lincoln Court narrative
supportExplanation: The FBI retrospective provides the report and confrontation sequence.
qualification: An agency retrospective, not an independently checked floor plan or a full set of witness statements.

assertion: Evelyn Frechette was convicted of conspiracy to harbor a federal fugitive, sentenced to two years and fined $1,000.
locators: S11, Frechette paragraph
supportExplanation: The FBI retrospective reports the conviction and sentence; an original judgment has not been examined here.
qualification: Specific legal charge was harboring a fugitive, not participating in bank heists.

assertion: Saint Paul's former federal courthouse (now Landmark Center) served as the venue for Frechette's trial.
locators: S14, closing caption and historical notes
supportExplanation: Library of Congress history identifies Landmark Center as the trial location.
qualification: Building association established; specific courtroom chamber unverified.

assertion: A wiretap investigation exposed Saint Paul police corruption in 1935 and led to disciplinary action.
locators: S12, wiretap investigation paragraph
supportExplanation: MNHS account describes clandestine telephone taps revealing officer complicity with underworld figures.
qualification: Attributed to the MNHS account. This project does not establish that this was a federal wiretap operation.

assertion: Saint Paul voters approved a charter amendment on June 15, 1936 instituting civil service rules for police chief selection and tenure.
locators: S12, amendment paragraphs
supportExplanation: MNHS history details the transition from political appointment to competitive examination and 6-year terms.
qualification: Structural administrative reform; did not instantly eradicate all vice.

assertion: Ma Barker functioned as the criminal mastermind and tactical leader of the Barker-Karpis gang.
locators: S02, discussion of gang leadership
supportExplanation: The examined historical account disputes treating Ma Barker as the operational mastermind. This does not establish a complete origin history for that portrayal.
qualification: Disputed folklore; do not present as an established historical fact.

assertion: Minnesota Historical Society interprets the Hamm and Bremer kidnappings as the breakdown of the O'Connor layover arrangement.
locators: S02, kidnapping breakdown paragraph
supportExplanation: Historical analysis views violent local kidnappings as shattering the covenant of immunity within the city.
qualification: Historical interpretation; reflects the erosion of boundaries rather than a single sudden decree.

assertion: Nick Hannegraf identified Alvin Karpis and Fred Barker as his mother’s West St. Paul tenants after recognizing them in a detective magazine.
locators: S17, April 30, 1932 report, printed pp. 4–5, Hannegraf account and rental address | S18, 1932 West St. Paul rental and recognition in True Detective Mysteries.
supportExplanation: The state report records Hannegraf’s identification and the South Robert Street address. MNopedia recounts the recognition.
qualification: The period report supplies the historical rental address. It does not establish present-day access.

assertion: Hannegraf said the departing tenants left the door open, the gas on, the radio playing, and part of a meal on the table.
locators: S17, April 30, 1932 report, printed pp. 4–5, Hannegraf account and rental address | S10, Printed pp. 5–6, report of recognition, violin case, and departure.
supportExplanation: The Minnesota BCA records Hannegraf’s account. The later FBI reconstruction separately describes a violin case noticed by his mother.
qualification: These details come from witness accounts. The violin case’s contents are unknown, and the reports give different accounts of the departure sequence.

assertion: Frank Cloutier and the Victoria Café Orchestra recorded “Moonshiner’s Dance” at the Lowry Hotel in 1927.
locators: S19, track listing and recording | S20, printed pp. 146–151 and 162, party favors, recording date, and Lowry Hotel.
supportExplanation: The Smithsonian reissue preserves the recording. Gegenhuber locates the session at the Lowry Hotel and describes the café’s tin saxophone noisemakers.
qualification: The studio session took place at the hotel. The 1997 Smithsonian release is a reissue.

assertion: The Victoria Café faced a six-month closure in March 1928 and a separate federal raid in December.
locators: S20, printed pp. 162–165, padlock order, December raid, and reproduced newspaper and telegram.
supportExplanation: Gegenhuber traces the closure to Prohibition enforcement over mixers served to customers who brought liquor. His account records McGill’s altercation with an agent in December and reproduces the front page and a telegram.
qualification: The incidents took place months apart. The account attributes McGill’s explanation to him.

assertion: John Quinn was convicted of second-degree murder in Frank Ventress’s death behind the Green Lantern, and the Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the conviction.
locators: S21, Reporter pp. 243–244 and 249–253, account of shooting and ruling on Quinn’s appeal.
supportExplanation: The appeal identifies the scene, summarizes Quinn’s self-defense argument and trial testimony, and affirms the judgment.
qualification: The opinion is used for the facts and outcome of the case as it records them.

assertion: A researcher proposed that a set of old police photographs depicted the Green Lantern.
locators: S22, Reproduced April 13, 2019 article and photographs, case mark X-40, exterior date, and photo identifications.
supportExplanation: Woltman reports how Neuberger and Sazevich used the synagogue pillar ornament and describes how the booths and menu board matched witnesses’ descriptions.
qualification: An exterior view marked X-40 bears a date before the shooting. The proposed identification and any use as trial exhibits remain unresolved.

assertion: The FBI summary records three prison escapes by Edna Murray, including an escape with Irene McCann in December 1932.
locators: S10, Printed pp. 10–11, robbery conviction and escapes | S23, Front-page coverage of the 1925 robbery case and Murray’s nickname.
supportExplanation: The summary describes the earlier robbery conviction and sawing through the cell bars. The 1925 newspaper documents Murray’s nickname in the press.
qualification: The nickname is documented. The alleged kiss remains unverified.

assertion: The federal charges against Edna Murray in the Bremer proceedings in Saint Paul were dismissed in May 1935.
locators: S10, Printed pp. 44–46, trial and dismissal.
supportExplanation: The investigation summary records the trial, dismissal, and return to Missouri to serve time in the earlier case and for the escape.
qualification: The Missouri robbery conviction was a separate case.

assertion: The FBI’s Bremer summary describes three men having facial and fingertip surgery near Toledo.
locators: S10, Printed p. 33, facial and fingertip surgery.
supportExplanation: The summary names Arthur Barker, Volney Davis, and Harry Campbell and says companions, including Edna Murray, had to feed them while their fingers hurt.
qualification: These details come from the investigators’ reconstruction.

assertion: A gasoline can with a fingerprint attributed to Arthur Barker was introduced at the Bremer trial in Saint Paul.
locators: S10, Printed p. 45, admission of the gasoline can | S18, Bremer investigation and discarded gasoline can.
supportExplanation: The investigation summary describes admission of the can over defense objection. MNopedia recounts its discovery by a Wisconsin farmer.
qualification: The discovery detail comes from a later historical account. The Bremer trial exhibit was separate from the Hamm case.

assertion: The August 30, 1933 Swift and Company payroll robbery in South St. Paul killed officer Leo Pavlak.
locators: S24, Account of the August 30, 1933 payroll robbery and officers who were shot | S10, Printed p. 14, Swift payroll robbery and notebook route.
supportExplanation: The later Minnesota House account describes the robbery outside the post office and Pavlak’s death. The FBI summary describes the robbery and the officers who were shot.
qualification: The cited accounts differ on the amount taken.

assertion: Federal investigators concluded that a route in a notebook found in Cleveland matched the South St. Paul payroll robbery getaway.
locators: S25, Printed p. 5, agents’ description of tracing the route | S10, Printed p. 14, Swift payroll robbery and notebook route.
supportExplanation: The FBI memorandum and Bremer summary describe tracing the notebook route back to Stockyards National Bank.
qualification: The identification comes from investigators. The cited documents describe the chart in prose.

assertion: Jack Peifer told federal agents that Frank Nash and his wife had dined at the Hollyhocks Inn shortly before Nash died.
locators: S26, October 13, 1934 memorandum, St. Paul File 62-888, summarizing the October 11 interview with Jack Pfeiffer | S27, June 17, 1933 section, Union Station attack and Nash’s death.
supportExplanation: The interview memorandum records Peifer’s recollection and places the dinner about ten days before Nash’s death. The FBI case history dates the Kansas City Massacre.
qualification: Peifer supplied the account of the dinner. The linked sources do not independently establish the visit.

assertion: Jack Peifer received a 30-year sentence in the William Hamm kidnapping case and died on July 31, 1936.
locators: S26, October 13, 1934 memorandum, St. Paul File 62-888, summarizing the October 11 interview with Jack Pfeiffer | S28, Front page, Associated Press report on Peifer’s sentence and death.
supportExplanation: The Associated Press dispatch reports the jury conviction, sentence, and death that day. The earlier interview records his separate denial of knowledge of the Kansas City killing.
qualification: The cases were separate. Accounts differ on details of Peifer’s last hours.

assertion: The FBI later said an agent used a necktie to bind Alvin Karpis’s hands during his New Orleans arrest.
locators: S29, May 1, 2012, Canal Street arrest and necktie paragraphs.
supportExplanation: The FBI’s 2012 account dates the arrest to May 1, 1936 and describes agents arriving without handcuffs.
qualification: The necktie detail comes from the FBI’s retrospective account.

assertion: Alvin Karpis was brought to Saint Paul after his arrest and later received a life sentence after pleading guilty in the Hamm case.
locators: S30, p. 5, May 2 Associated Press dispatch | S10, printed p. 54, Hamm plea and sentence.
supportExplanation: The Associated Press dispatch reported his arrival by plane. The investigation summary records his plea and sentence.
qualification: The contemporary article concerns his arrival. The plea and sentence are documented separately.

assertion: A surviving April 1908 receipt records a mayoral wager between Richard T. O’Connor and Philip W. Herzog.
locators: S31, Printed p. 23, receipt MNHS P1190-27 reproduced.
supportExplanation: The receipt reproduced in Minnesota History gives the candidates, stakes, and the clause voiding the wager if either bettor or candidate died before the election.
qualification: The published image reproduces the period document. Whether the wager was paid remains unknown.

assertion: The wager receipt was signed by Herzog and addressed to Pierce Butler, who later served on the U.S. Supreme Court.
locators: S31, Printed pp. 19 and 22–23, participants and receipt.
supportExplanation: Osten identifies the participants and supplies their political and professional context alongside the receipt.
qualification: The paper names Butler as addressee. His role in handling the wager remains unclear.

assertion: The 1997 Science Museum excavation uncovered the foundations of Nina Clifford’s brothel and artifacts from the property.
locators: S32, Site 21RA32, discovery and artifact comparison paragraphs | S33, Ketz, Abel and Schmidt, Historical Archaeology 39(1), pp. 74–88, abstract.
supportExplanation: The excavation summary and the archaeological study describe material recovered at the site and differences between the lives of customers and residents.
qualification: Food and tableware evidence support interpretations about life at this site. The health findings concern its residents as studied by the researchers.

assertion: The Minnesota Historical Society reports that excavators found no tunnel linking Nina Clifford’s brothel to the Minnesota Club.
locators: S34, Concluding biography paragraphs, excavation and tunnel legend.
supportExplanation: MNopedia describes the local rumor and the excavation’s outcome.
qualification: The result describes the area the team investigated.

assertion: Helen Warren Pfleger recalled working at the Saint Paul Prohibition Office from 1925.
locators: S35, Printed pp. 19–21, office work, switchboard, and clothes.
supportExplanation: Her memoir describes her office role, staying late to cover the switchboard, and agents dressing in worn clothes for fieldwork.
qualification: This is a later recollection of her own work.

assertion: Pfleger’s memoir recounts an agent finding a faucet that dispensed liquor behind a flower shop’s fern display.
locators: S35, Printed p. 21, flower shop anecdote.
supportExplanation: Pfleger tells the story in her 1975 memoir as an incident involving an investigator.
qualification: The memoir gives a secondhand account. The shop, date, and enforcement outcome remain unidentified.

assertion: Federal agents reported finding a body-rub redistilling plant and supplies for bottling liquor as Scotch at a Saint Paul bungalow in 1925.
locators: S36, Printed p. 15, reproduced June 27 St. Paul Daily News caption and following Pioneer Press and seizure passages.
supportExplanation: Gold reproduces the Daily News caption naming the location, doors and reported ingredient and recounts the bottling equipment and labels.
qualification: The plant and contents are presented as the agents’ account in period coverage reproduced by Gold.

assertion: Gold’s history reports that all but one bottle had been destroyed by agents by the time Sam Taran went to trial and that the jury acquitted him.
locators: S36, Printed p. 15, paragraph beginning “Taran’s trial for his operation on Wheeler Avenue”.
supportExplanation: The account names the October 22 trial, destruction of bottles, defense argument, and not-guilty verdict.
qualification: The source leaves the reason for the destruction unresolved. The verdict was an acquittal in the Wheeler Avenue case.

assertion: A July 1932 Associated Press dispatch reported Haskell Bohn’s kidnapping in Saint Paul and described a $35,000 ransom note written in pencil.
locators: S37, Printed p. 3, “Youth Seized by Kidnapers for Ransom,” opening paragraphs and description of note.
supportExplanation: The period dispatch describes Bohn’s age, the location of his abduction, the note’s delivery and the demand.
qualification: The amount demanded and the amount ultimately paid are separate questions.

assertion: Police told the AP that a dummy package was used to catch three men suspected of a separate attempt to obtain money from Bohn’s father.
locators: S38, Printed p. 3, “Ransom Not Paid for Bohn,” father’s denial and final paragraph on the dummy package | S39, Home edition p. 1, “Bohn Case Arrest,” indictment and alleged payment.
supportExplanation: The AP attributes the trap to police and records the father’s denial. The later newspaper separately describes allegations in the kidnapping indictment.
qualification: The alleged extortion and the kidnapping were separate matters. The examined reports establish neither the three men’s legal outcomes nor a settled ransom amount.

assertion: Agent Hardy’s January 1936 report traced Sawyer’s Minneapolis arrest under the name Harry Stanley and identified a fingerprint card and photograph plate.
locators: S40, January 25 report, pp. 1–2, beginning “On January 21, 1936,” arrest, detectives’ account, and fingerprint clerk.
supportExplanation: The report explains the prosecutor’s request and records the police file, clerk’s offer and detectives’ recollections.
qualification: The report describes the card and plate and records a later recollection about the warning shot.

assertion: The court entries reproduced by Hardy recorded a misdemeanor plea and payment of a fine. The prosecutor told Hardy the old conviction could not be used to impeach Sawyer.
locators: S40, January 25 report, pp. 2–3, reproduced court entries and Sullivan’s response.
supportExplanation: The agent reproduces the lesser charge, plea and payment and records the prosecutor’s response after the search.
qualification: The reported misdemeanor is the outcome of this case. The earlier arrest classification describes a different stage of the same case.

assertion: Federal agents reported using baggage to track Eddie Green after the Lincoln Court shootout. Green died after agents shot him in Saint Paul.
locators: S41, April 10 memorandum beginning “I have just been advised that Eugene Green,” filing stamp 62-29777-4721 | S42, Front-page AP dispatch beginning “ST. PAUL, Minn., Aug. 24,” paragraph mentioning Green’s fatal shooting.
supportExplanation: The federal memorandum recounts the route of the baggage and the encounter. The AP dispatch independently records that federal agents fatally wounded Green in Saint Paul.
qualification: The baggage trail follows the agents’ account. An exact shooting address is omitted because the paperwork gives conflicting addresses.

assertion: The Bureau recorded Green’s statement that the keys belonged to Dillinger and described an apparent fit between a gunstock and a gun from Lincoln Court.
locators: S41, April 10 memorandum, filing stamp 62-29777-4721, passages on keys and gunstock.
supportExplanation: The Bureau’s memo attributes the keys to Green’s statement and treats the stock’s fit as an observation.
qualification: The memo supplies the agents’ account of Green’s statement and an apparent fit. It establishes neither object’s independent identification.

assertion: The 1936 federal investigation summary attributed the McCord shooting to gang members who mistook airline employees for police and linked it to a delay in the Bremer kidnapping plan.
locators: S10, Printed p. 17, paragraph beginning “The gang had originally planned”.
supportExplanation: The summary names the employer, intersection, date, injury, and Sawyer’s reported response.
qualification: The shooters’ reasoning and Sawyer’s role in delaying the plan are the investigators’ reconstruction.

assertion: Roy McCord survived his injuries and told federal agents he could not identify Arthur Barker as the shooter.
locators: S43, Printed p. 111, paragraph beginning “Later, during the same day, Roy McCord” | S44, “Gangsters gone bad,” paragraphs on the January shooting and recovery.
supportExplanation: The 1935 report describes the unsuccessful identification. The later account names McCord, describes his occupation and reports his recovery.
qualification: The 1936 summary calls the victim P. N. McCord. The earlier federal report and the later press account use Roy McCord. His inability to identify Barker does not identify another shooter.

assertion: Abe and Ben Gleeman were convicted of first-degree murder for the fatal shooting of Burton Stevens at a Saint Paul drugstore corner in February 1925.
supportExplanation: The court states the convictions and life sentences, gives the time and location of the shooting, and describes the appeal.
qualification: The opinion records the convictions and separates them from the parties’ accounts of how the shooting happened.

assertion: The Gleemans’ unsuccessful bid for a new trial included allegations about a railroad car of alcohol, a shipment to an Eighth Street garage, and a different shooter.
supportExplanation: The opinion recounts the brothers’ new account and explains the decision to affirm the lower court’s orders.
qualification: The railcar, truck shipment, and alternative shooter are attributed to the defense account. The court allowed the verdicts to stand.

assertion: Cooke testified that Wynn followed him to his basement furnace and said the man accompanying Wynn was there to guard him.
locators: S46, Printed pp. 180–182, Cooke’s account of the conversation by the furnace | S36, Printed p. 16, paragraph beginning “Taran’s dealings at the Wynn Motors auto dealership.”.
supportExplanation: The opinion recounts Cooke’s testimony. Gold places Wynn Motors at 706 University Avenue in Saint Paul.
qualification: Cooke recalled what Wynn told him. The companion’s role was Wynn’s account.

assertion: The Minnesota Supreme Court upheld Sam Taran’s grand larceny conviction over a $700 auto finance transaction in 1929.
locators: S46, Printed pp. 176–180 and 183, the Otas Finance Company transaction, independent evidence of proceeds, and affirmed judgment.
supportExplanation: The opinion describes the $700 check and finds independent evidence that Taran received the proceeds. It also summarizes Wynn’s coercion testimony.
qualification: The judgment covers the finance transaction. The claimed ten days of detention come from Wynn’s testimony.

assertion: Alice McQuillan Dunn was murdered at her family’s Saint Paul home, where her rings and watch were left behind, and accomplices testified that the killing was meant to look like a burglary.
supportExplanation: The opinion recounts the shooting, lists the valuables left behind, and summarizes the accomplices’ account of the plan and the taxi detour.
qualification: The plan and payment terms are testimony summarized by the court. A small amount of cash was taken from a different room.

assertion: Frank Dunn was convicted of first-degree murder, and the Minnesota Supreme Court found enough corroborating evidence to uphold the denial of a new trial.
supportExplanation: The opinion states the outcome and describes how Dunn’s own admissions fit parts of the accomplices’ testimony.
qualification: The prosecution inferred that the money used to pay the men came from the vault. Dunn offered a different explanation for his visit.

assertion: Herbert Scott recalled that he and Boyd Carrier took a .45 automatic from Tommy Carroll and turned him over to detectives.
locators: S48, printed pp. 17–18, Scott’s account of working with Boyd Carrier on Robert Street.
supportExplanation: Scott describes the call on Robert Street, taking the pistol, and turning Carroll over to the Detective Division.
qualification: This is Scott’s recollection decades later. The date of the encounter and the detectives’ reasons remain unknown.

assertion: Scott recalled seeing Carroll with what he recognized as the same gun and later being unable to find Carrier’s report.
locators: S48, Printed p. 18, Carroll’s return to Robert Street and Carrier’s report.
supportExplanation: Scott recalls the street encounter about two hours later and says Carrier filed a report they later could not find.
qualification: Scott does not establish how Carroll got the gun, who authorized his release, or what happened to the report.

assertion: Bernice Fisher remembered watching police run up the alley across from her childhood home on the day Van Meter was killed.
locators: S49, Printed p. 25, the family’s address and the sentence beginning “I stood on the front porch.” | S42, Front page, Saint Paul dispatch dated August 24, reporting Van Meter was killed the previous night and identifying his Dillinger association.
supportExplanation: Fisher gives her childhood address and recalls the scene from the porch. The contemporary dispatch identifies Van Meter as a Dillinger associate and dates his death.
qualification: Fisher’s account is a later memory of the officers’ movements. Her memoir misidentifies Van Meter’s gang.

assertion: Scott recalled responding to a call about an injured dog before hearing gunfire and finding Van Meter behind a filling station.
locators: S48, Printed pp. 19–20, the dog call and Scott’s account of where Van Meter was found.
supportExplanation: Scott recalls the dog call, the shots to the east, and the alley behind a filling station near Marion and University.
qualification: The interviewer and Scott gave different cross streets for the dog call. The recollection does not establish who fired first.

assertion: The Senate report on the Rogowskis’ refund claim records the inspector’s description, John Rogowski’s plea and fine, and the brothers’ payment of the assessment under protest.
locators: S50, S. Rept. 2052, printed pp. 2–4, inspector’s description, and pp. 16–18, Representative Ryan’s letter.
supportExplanation: The committee papers reproduce the inspector’s description and record the fine and assessment. Representative Ryan’s letter gives the initial quantity and price alleged.
qualification: The inspector reported a surname and physical description. The identity of the bartender was disputed.

assertion: A Senate committee recommended reimbursing the Rogowskis. President Roosevelt withheld approval of H.R. 4941.
locators: S50, S. Rept. 2052, printed pp. 1–4 and 16–18, committee recommendation and Representative Ryan’s letter | S51, Congressional Record, 75th Congress, vol. 83, printed pp. 9714–9715, H.R. 4941 message.
supportExplanation: The Senate report records the mistaken identity argument and recommendation. Roosevelt’s message records his refusal and reasons.
qualification: The papers preserve a disputed identification. They leave the actual seller unresolved.

assertion: The Raasch opinion describes how calls from a line that bypassed the police switchboard were recorded and replayed for jurors after the needle skipped.
locators: S52, Printed pp. 159–161, paragraphs 2–4, Cedar 5328, pamograph, headsets and playback.
supportExplanation: The court describes the line, recording mechanism, listening equipment, and replay procedure.
qualification: The opinion describes the recordings used in court. The individual call dates and the present location of the recordings remain unresolved.

assertion: The Raasch opinion distinguishes the admitted recordings from the transcripts used at trial and affirms the denial of a new trial following his malfeasance conviction.
locators: S52, Printed pp. 160–162, paragraphs 3–8, admission of recordings, use of transcripts, and disposition.
supportExplanation: The opinion finds a sufficient foundation for the recordings, describes the use of typed copies, and affirms the order.
qualification: The court reviewed Raasch’s conviction and the handling of evidence in his case.

assertion: The FBI recorded and reported corroboration of Bolton’s account of the July 23, 1933 flight and his leaving it at Madison.
locators: S53, March 16, 1936 memorandum, first page, paragraph about Bolton and Northwest Airways.
supportExplanation: The memo dates the trip and describes the passenger manifests and Agent Coulter’s statement as corroboration.
qualification: The surviving memo gives no reason for Bolton’s trip or his departure in Madison. It does not establish whether Hamm saw him.

assertion: The FBI’s summary identifies Bolton as a participant in the Hamm kidnapping, and a contemporary court report records his prior plea and expected testimony.
locators: S10, Printed pp. 13–14, Hamm kidnapping and Bolton’s association with Fred Goetz | S54, Printed p. 5, “Remaining Defendants,” paragraph about Bolton and Fitzgerald.
supportExplanation: The FBI summary names Bolton in the abduction and describes how he was invited to participate. The dispatch places his guilty plea and expected testimony in the Hamm proceedings.
qualification: The testimony reference reflects the prosecutor’s expectation as reported at the time.

assertion: Federal agents testified that they bought moonshine at the storefront and that one of the keys Weinberg said was for his car opened a courtyard door.
locators: S55, Printed pp. 415–416, agents’ accounts of purchases and Weinberg’s keys.
supportExplanation: The opinion records the purchase testimony and the agents’ description of opening the locked door with a key Weinberg produced.
qualification: These are the agents’ accounts as recounted by the court. The defendants disputed their testimony.

assertion: The Weinberg opinion records the agents’ inventory, the defense’s denial, the guilty verdicts, and the court’s denial of the application for a writ of error.
locators: S55, Printed pp. 416–418, inventory, defense testimony and verdicts, and p. 422, denial of application.
supportExplanation: The judge summarizes the competing accounts, identifies the possession and sale verdicts, and rules on the application.
qualification: The ruling concerns these defendants and these charges. The record supplies no named gang connection.

assertion: The FBI’s reconstruction places a Shell-marked Chevrolet and the next ransom instructions at 969 University Avenue.
locators: S10, Printed p. 23, February 6 transfer and note in the coupe.
supportExplanation: The case summary identifies the date, street address, marked coupe and contents of the door pocket.
qualification: The signs identify how the car appeared. Their presence establishes no role for Shell in the handoff.

assertion: The Bureau recorded the light signals and roadside deposit in the Bremer ransom handoff and followed up on the Shell signs.
locators: S10, Printed pp. 23–24, instructions and Magee’s account of following the bus and leaving the money | S56, PDF p. 38, paragraphs on the original sign and sign painters’ union.
supportExplanation: The case summary reproduces the directions and reconstructs the drive. The field report records showing the sign to a sign writer and the union contact.
qualification: The records do not identify the driver who flashed the lights or the sign’s maker.

assertion: The FBI recorded Bremer’s recollection of the wallpaper and reported obtaining a similar specimen from a pattern sold by a mail-order house.
locators: S10, Printed p. 24, paragraphs on Bremer’s observations and the wallpaper specimen.
supportExplanation: The summary credits Bremer with describing the wallpaper and records the agents’ search and his comparison with their sample.
qualification: The summary describes similarity. The specimen by itself does not establish the location of the room.

assertion: Bremer recalled sounds, food and a damaged flush lever from his captivity, as recorded in the FBI’s case summary.
locators: S10, Printed pp. 24–25, dogs and children, toilet lever with damaged enamel, and the strawberry shortcake.
supportExplanation: The summary records Bremer’s sensory observations and his recollection of fresh strawberry shortcake.
qualification: The source records what Bremer reported and leaves the cook’s identity unresolved.

assertion: A federal investigator’s letter records the identification of Frank Nash’s right thumbprint on a beer bottle recovered at 804 Vernon Avenue.
locators: S57, January 31, 1934 letter from John Hanni, file 62-888, quoting the June 23, 1933 Western Union telegram.
supportExplanation: Hanni identifies the object and address and quotes the federal identification of the print.
qualification: The match does not establish when or where Nash touched the bottle.

assertion: The federal report records a search for the source of six Squeezor beer bottles and says police kept the one with Nash’s print.
locators: S58, Internal p. 14, paragraphs beginning “Considerable time was spent interviewing shop keepers” and “At the St. Clair Street shop.”.
supportExplanation: The report names the two nearby shops that sold the brand and describes the unsuccessful search. Local officers said they were preserving the bottle with Nash’s print.
qualification: The documented canvass did not identify who bought the bottles or where they were sold.

assertion: The FBI linked De Vol’s Saint Paul apartment to money from a fatal Minneapolis bank robbery and recorded his murder plea and life sentence.
locators: S10, Printed p. 10, Third Northwestern National Bank robbery and De Vol’s arrest and plea | S59, Printed p. 5, “Bank Robbery Suspects Held,” Saint Paul apartment and recovered proceeds.
supportExplanation: The FBI summary describes the robbery, deaths and plea. The contemporary wire report names Barton and attributes the recovery of proceeds in his apartment to the authorities.
qualification: The contemporary dispatch distinguishes the county attorney’s account of Barton’s statement from Barton’s refusal to admit taking part in the raid.

assertion: Contemporary papers reported that De Vol escaped from St. Peter and described a barred window and fire hose in the breakout.
locators: S60, Printed p. 3, continuation reporting chair legs, tools, barred window and hose | S61, Printed p. 1, St. Peter dispatch on the evening breakout and De Vol.
supportExplanation: The contemporary coverage identifies De Vol as an escapee and reports the method used by the group.
qualification: The reports do not establish whether De Vol personally handled the chair legs, tools or hose.

assertion: A period clipping reports the attack on Taran, and Paul R. Gold’s account says Alexander was thrown down a staircase and taken to Ancker Hospital.
locators: S36, Printed p. 16 (PDF page 6), “Former Pugilist Shot” clipping and paragraph beginning “That Christmas Eve.”.
supportExplanation: Gold reproduces the clipping that reports Taran’s injury and gives the staircase and hospital details in his own narrative.
qualification: The clipping supports the attack and Taran’s injury. The staircase and identification of Alexander come from Gold’s later account.

assertion: Gold reports that Billy Alexander left Ancker Hospital in slippers, pajamas, and a robe in January 1926.
locators: S36, Printed p. 16 (PDF page 6), paragraph beginning “Around midnight on January 21, 1926.”.
supportExplanation: Gold gives the date, clothing and temperature and reports the police theory about a car.
qualification: The escape details come from Gold’s later account. The waiting car was a police theory.

assertion: A federal letter records a conversation between Brennan and Tierney about a purported recording and says Tierney denied the allegation.
locators: S62, March 14 confidential letter, from “On March 13” through the paragraph containing “Tierney vehemently denied”.
supportExplanation: Stein recounts Brennan raising the claim and Tierney denying the alleged conversation.
qualification: The letter preserves the accusation and denial. It leaves the existence and contents of any recording unresolved.

assertion: Stein’s letter says Tierney asked to hear the alleged record or obtain a retraction and that Brennan declined to go to the newspaper.
locators: S62, March 14 confidential letter, Tierney’s proposal about Kahn through the O. W. Stein signature.
supportExplanation: The letter describes Tierney’s demand, Brennan’s response, and Tierney’s offer to cooperate.
qualification: Stein relays the interview. The year of the letter is uncertain in the available text.

assertion: A 1936 Daily News editorial attributes statements about a gold exchange, a $1,000 bill, loans, and safe-deposit boxes to Thomas Brown at a civil service hearing.
locators: S63, September 24, 1936 “Brown Hearing” editorial, passages on Brown’s statements and assets.
supportExplanation: The contemporary editorial lists figures and transactions it attributes to Brown’s hearing testimony.
qualification: The source is a newspaper editorial about the hearing. The signed findings and underlying financial records are outside this account.

assertion: The editorial compared Brown’s reported assets and transactions with his police salary and allowed that they could be explained.
locators: S63, September 24, 1936 “Brown Hearing” editorial, salary comparison and acknowledgment of a possible explanation.
supportExplanation: The editorial supplies its reported salary figure, exception for Brown’s service as chief, and express acknowledgment that an explanation might exist.
qualification: The editorial raises a question about Brown’s finances. The origin of the money and any finding of wrongdoing remain unestablished by this source.

assertion: A 1936 opinion recounts police finding chilled beer and two slot machines on rubber pads in Kaasa’s apartment.
locators: S64, Printed p. 182, account of the March 19 search, the beer, glasses and slot machines.
supportExplanation: The opinion describes the entry and lists what officers said they found in the kitchen and front room.
qualification: The inventory is evidence in a liquor-license case. The opinion does not give a reason for the rubber pads.

assertion: The Minnesota Supreme Court upheld Kaasa’s conviction for keeping liquor for sale without a city license.
locators: S64, Printed pp. 182–184, Kaasa’s account, absence of a search warrant or proof of an actual sale, and disposition.
supportExplanation: The opinion records Kaasa’s explanation, describes the evidence and affirms the judgment.
qualification: The judgment concerns unlicensed liquor. It does not record a gambling conviction.

assertion: Mystic Caverns advertised two thousand mirrors, Jack Foster’s Ten Cavemen, and directions to a neon skull and crossbones.
locators: S07, Printed p. 113, April 14, 1933 St. Paul Daily News advertisement and adjoining discussion.
supportExplanation: Brick reproduces a period ad and transcribes advertising copy for the mirrors, band and directions.
qualification: The advertising establishes the promise. The actual number of mirrors is unverified.

assertion: Brick links Mystic Caverns’ 1934 closure to a gambling investigation, and an archival finding aid identifies a casino operator at the venue.
locators: S07, Printed p. 114, Foster’s police band role, the grand jury investigation, and the distinction from Castle Royal | S65, Alphabetical research files, entry for Robert “Frisco Dutch” Steinhardt.
supportExplanation: Brick recounts the investigation and closure. The finding aid separately identifies the subject of a file as a casino operator at Mystic Caverns.
qualification: The finding aid identifies an archive subject and does not establish an individual verdict.

assertion: Whittier described Dayton’s Saint Paul shop and a job proposal for the newly paroled Younger brothers.
locators: S66, July 18, 1901 Whittier to Wolfer, passage beginning “his present store located on Wabasha”.
supportExplanation: The letter gives the location, fixtures, dimensions, and proposed employment.
qualification: The letter describes a proposal and does not establish acceptance.

assertion: Whittier described a card game using checks that Dayton sold for five cents and redeemed for five cents in goods or two and a half cents in cash.
locators: S66, July 18, 1901 letter, paragraph beginning “As to the rumor of gambling”.
supportExplanation: The letter records the game, the ten-cent payment, and the two redemption rates.
qualification: Dayton’s explanation is attributed to him. The letter gives no criminal finding about the game and supplies no physical description of the checks.

assertion: Dayton proposed a monthly guarantee and a possible profit share. Other records identify Jim Younger at Andrew Schoch Grocery’s cigar department.
locators: S66, July 18, 1901 letter, terms of Dayton’s job proposal | S67, Files 633–634, undated Globe Hotel card | S68, Chapter 34, “On Parole,” Jim’s work for Andrew Schoch Grocery.
supportExplanation: Whittier gives the terms. The advertising card and memoir identify Jim’s cigar work at Schoch’s.
qualification: The advertising card is undated. These sources establish neither acceptance of Dayton’s offer nor participation by either brother in the card game.

assertion: Agents took freight papers and a special-delivery envelope addressed to Gleckman when they arrested truck driver Sol Rosenhause.
locators: S69, ¶¶ 27–31, papers taken from Rosenhause, Globe Building address and delivery timing.
supportExplanation: The appeals opinion describes the seizure, lists the papers, and gives the envelope’s destination and delivery date.
qualification: The opinion describes the envelope. Its physical appearance beyond the described markings is unresolved.

assertion: The bills of lading described later shipments of “Aleo Wash” to West Side Pharmacy, and the court described the use of the pharmacy’s name to receive alcohol.
locators: S69, ¶¶ 24–35, pharmacy arrangement, bills of lading, and dates the incoming freight arrived.
supportExplanation: The court identifies the shipper, consignee and description on the bills, and places delivery after the seizure.
qualification: The freight on the bills and the load in the stopped truck were separate. The opinion expresses doubt about the druggist’s knowledge of the plant.

assertion: The Eighth Circuit inferred that Gleckman passed the envelope to Rosenhause and affirmed the judgment after Gleckman sought to withdraw his guilty plea.
locators: S69, ¶¶ 27–35 on the envelope, procedural history and ¶ 51 on disposition.
supportExplanation: The opinion explains the inference, records the plea and request to withdraw it, and affirms the judgment.
qualification: The handoff was the court’s inference from the paperwork. The judgment concerns the liquor case.

assertion: An April 25 FBI phone slip records that a news service reported a possible capture of Alvin Karpis in the West.
locators: S70, April 25, 1935 call slip, 8:15 p.m. entry.
supportExplanation: The entry records Suydam’s name, the news service’s report and his inability to give a specific place.
qualification: The slip establishes the content of the call. The reported capture remained unconfirmed.

assertion: The same FBI slip records that Suydam changed the reported region to the East, attributed the report to Saint Paul and that the local office had not heard about it.
locators: S70, 8:25 p.m. entry and final paragraph on the call to Saint Paul.
supportExplanation: The two entries and follow-up preserve the change in direction and the response from the local office.
qualification: The slip does not name the original source in Saint Paul or establish whether the story was published.

assertion: The FBI dates the documented New Orleans arrest to May 1, 1936, over a year after the April 25, 1935 calls.
locators: S09, “The Big Fish is Caught,” capture and return, and opening photo caption for the date | S70, April 25, 1935 date and two reported locations.
supportExplanation: The call slip dates the rumor. The FBI’s case history gives the date and place of the actual arrest and the immediate transfer to Saint Paul.
qualification: The records give no connection between the rumor and the arrest operation.

assertion: A 1936 United Press dispatch reports that Robbins worked on a portable refrigerator while serving a 25-year term in the Gleckman kidnapping case.
locators: S71, Printed p. 3, “Kidnaper In Prison Works On Invention,” opening paragraphs.
supportExplanation: The dispatch identifies Robbins, his term and the kidnapping, and describes the design.
qualification: The sentence and Robbins’s role are reported in the dispatch. A sentencing judgment was not examined.

assertion: United Press reports that Robbins began the design before sentencing and envisioned it for hunters, fishermen, motorists and picnickers.
locators: S71, Printed p. 3, same brief, passage on when the design started and whom Robbins expected to use it.
supportExplanation: The dispatch gives the timeline and lists the practical uses.
qualification: The brief gives no drawing, patent or finished example of the design.

assertion: The newspaper reported that Robbins put his refrigerator plans before the state pardon board in connection with a commutation request.
locators: S71, Printed p. 3, same brief, passage on the pardon board and commutation.
supportExplanation: The dispatch links the plans to a request for commutation.
qualification: The board’s disposition is unverified.

assertion: Federal records describe Davis’s escape after a forced landing. A contemporary agent’s diary describes the phone call, removal of shackles and flight by car.
locators: S72, February 6, 1935 entry, forced landing and escape | S10, Printed p. 43, opening paragraph on Davis’s arrest and escape.
supportExplanation: The diary and the later case summary both describe the landing and escape. The diary supplies the more specific account of what happened in town.
qualification: McDade’s diary dates the escape to February 6. The later case summary gives February 7.

assertion: The FBI reported recovering a counterfeit $100 bill and recorded Davis’s account of why he carried it.
locators: S10, Printed p. 43, passage about the counterfeit $100 and Davis’s explanation.
supportExplanation: The summary distinguishes what agents recovered, what Davis said he intended and what he did when agents caught him.
qualification: The intended use was Davis’s explanation to investigators.

assertion: Davis returned to Saint Paul after his Chicago recapture, pleaded guilty to conspiracy and received a life sentence. An Associated Press dispatch describes his handcuffed escort.
locators: S73, Printed p. 1, second Saint Paul dateline and “Captured In Chicago” | S74, Printed pp. 407–408, motion and chronology of arrest, arraignment and sentence.
supportExplanation: The period report describes the escort and plea. The later court opinion supplies the recapture and sentencing dates.
qualification: The handcuff detail comes from contemporary news coverage.

assertion: Wolfer told Peterson he had heard that Bloom was passing himself off as Cole Younger and asked Peterson to intervene.
locators: S66, Wolfer letter, August 16, 1901, passage containing “passing himself off”.
supportExplanation: The warden names the salesman, summarizes what he heard, gives the towns, and asks Peterson to act.
qualification: The letter records a report from others. Bloom’s own account and sales pitch remain unverified.

assertion: Peterson told Wolfer he had written to Bloom to stop. Cole Younger later recalled working as a traveling salesman for Peterson.
locators: S66, Peterson to Wolfer, August 19, 1901, letterhead, body, and August 20 prison receipt stamp | S68, Chapter 34, “On Parole,” traveling for Peterson.
supportExplanation: Peterson records the intervention in his reply, and Younger’s memoir describes his employment with Peterson.
qualification: The letter records Peterson’s action as he described it. What Bloom did afterward remains unresolved.

assertion: The Tax Court found that Banks kept daily liquor sales in a vest-pocket book and did not keep a record of alcohol costs.
locators: S75, Findings of Fact, ¶ 23, daily sales and cost of alcohol.
supportExplanation: The opinion identifies the book as his only record for those years and describes what he wrote in it.
qualification: The 1961 opinion describes the book. The text of the book itself is not reproduced.

assertion: The Tax Court recorded Banks’s November 14, 1929 guilty plea on a liquor conspiracy charge in Saint Paul and his payment of a $2,500 fine.
locators: S75, Findings of Fact, ¶ 27, Saint Paul federal proceeding, plea and fine.
supportExplanation: The opinion names the date, charge, court division, amount and payment.
qualification: The findings do not establish that the pocketbook was used as evidence in the 1929 proceeding.

assertion: The Tax Court found that Banks ordered alcohol in boxcars with others and did not keep records for the West Hotel operation.
locators: S75, Findings of Fact, ¶¶ 24–26, typical shipments and West Hotel records.
supportExplanation: The opinion gives an approximate starting year, typical drum counts and the absence of books while he operated from the hotel.
qualification: The hotel operation was in Minneapolis. The opinion does not link an individual shipment to the earlier Saint Paul plea.

assertion: In one federal interview, Potthoff gave $331 as the initial and final trade-in allowance and said Gleeman requested black wire wheels.
locators: S76, Printed pp. 16–17, W. J. Potthoff interview
supportExplanation: Potthoff’s interview gives the dealership address, the negotiation and the proposed wheel change.
qualification: The file also contains an account of a separate Potthoff interview that gives $375 as the allowance on the transfer agreement.

assertion: Gleeman said the trade-in allowance rose from $331 to $375 and that Filben supplied the name for the order.
locators: S76, Printed pp. 16–20, vehicle identification, registration and Gleeman interview | S11, “The Bureau Actively Joins the Hunt,” the Hellman tenancy and March 31 escape
supportExplanation: Gleeman’s interview gives the two prices and describes the supplied name. The dealer interview and the FBI case history use the Hellman spelling.
qualification: The interviews give different final amounts and several spellings of the assumed surname.

assertion: The file gives $375 as the allowance on the transfer agreement, records Gleeman’s explanation of the $44 accounting difference, and identifies the Hudson as the car Dillinger had during his escape.
locators: S76, Gleeman question-and-answer immediately before printed p. 21 marker, plus the April 2 Notestein interview and its introductory paragraph immediately before the p. 50 marker
supportExplanation: The April 2 interview gives the transfer figure and delivery details, Gleeman’s interview gives the check and credit amounts, and the paragraph introducing the April 2 interview links the car to the escape.
qualification: The report describes the agreement. The reason for the difference between the check and the credit is Gleeman’s explanation. The file does not document every handoff to Dillinger.

assertion: Dorsey opened at 151 South Washington Street in March 1913 and reportedly testified to approaching Flanagan about her plans.
locators: S77, Main text, paragraph on the March 7, 1913 move to Saint Paul | S78, p. 167, Ida Dorsey section, and p. 213, chapter 5 note 29
supportExplanation: MNopedia gives the opening date and address. Petersen gives the meeting and references, citing the February 1914 local press.
qualification: Dorsey’s account of the meeting survives here through Petersen’s synthesis of trial reporting. The meeting details are attributed to Dorsey.

assertion: Clifford reportedly described $4,000 paid by Dorsey, with $1,000 for the house and $3,000 intended for protection.
locators: S78, p. 167, Clifford’s testimony and closing of the brothels, and p. 213, chapter 5 notes 29–30 | S77, Main text, paragraph on the $1,000 purchase and $3,000 protection payment
supportExplanation: Petersen summarizes the reported testimony and the closure. MNopedia also describes the purchase, protection payment, and closure.
qualification: The split comes from trial testimony reported in the press. The source leaves the complete distribution of the money unresolved. Petersen suggests the $1,000 may have been a down payment.

assertion: A contemporary Saint Paul dispatch reported the bribery convictions and prison sentences of Flanagan and Turner.
locators: S79, p. 2, ‘Chief and Detective Fined for Bribery,’ St. Paul, February 20 dateline | S78, p. 167, introduction to Ida Dorsey’s trial testimony
supportExplanation: The February 20 dispatch gives the jury verdict, names and sentences. Petersen independently records the two officials going to state prison as a result of the graft trial.
qualification: The dispatch describes a $300 charge and does not tie that figure to a particular portion of the $3,000 mentioned in Clifford’s reported testimony.

assertion: Federal records attribute the clothing to Bremer’s abductors and document a lab examination of its remaining marks, buttons and seams.
locators: S80, Report 360, February 14, 1934, archive-stamped pp. 121–122, shirt label, collar button, crayon mark and sock heel seams | S81, February 27, 1934 Saint Paul report, archive-stamped p. 128, paragraph on the clothing at Bremer’s release
supportExplanation: The Saint Paul field report gives the clothing’s origin; Appel’s report names the requesting office, specimens, dimensions and remaining details.
qualification: The measurements and markings come from the lab report. They do not identify who removed the label or bought the clothes.

assertion: The February 27 Saint Paul report lists two potential sellers after cross-indexing retailers for the clothes.
locators: S81, February 27, 1934 Saint Paul report, archive-stamped p. 128, paragraph naming Mueller Clothing and J. H. Conley
supportExplanation: The report explains the cross-index and names both businesses as possible sources for two of the garments.
qualification: The Windom lead was checked in person the following week. The list was a working index of retailers.

assertion: Ryan’s March 5 memo records Mueller’s reply that his merchandise did not match the shirt, underwear and socks.
locators: S82, W. C. Ryan’s March 5, 1934 memorandum for Saint Paul file 7-30, Gustave Mueller interview, before the March 6 memorandum
supportExplanation: Ryan records the shirt mismatch, the replacement sent for the underwear order and the absence of the sock brand.
qualification: The shopkeeper’s answers address the Windom lead. They do not settle where the kidnappers obtained the clothes.

assertion: The appellate opinion records the soft drink bar’s address, agents’ description of its saloon fittings and admitted Prohibition violations in April 1925.
locators: S83, Printed pp. 38–39, opening description, affidavits, stipulation and paragraph beginning “In this case the owner.”
supportExplanation: The opinion sets out the premises, affidavits and parties’ stipulation before identifying four sales on April 6 and possession on April 15.
qualification: The description of the fittings comes from the agents’ affidavits. The parties stipulated to the violations. The source establishes no organized-crime connection.

assertion: The stipulation records a change of tenant after the violations and no charges against the new tenant. The appeals court observed that the business continued with the same equipment.
locators: S83, Printed pp. 38–39, stipulation beginning “It is admitted by the complainant” and paragraph beginning “In this case the owner.”
supportExplanation: The stipulated facts identify the tenants, the date Ryshavy’s lease began and his record as stated in the proceeding. The court separately describes the continued use of the equipment.
qualification: The opinion records no conviction of Engler or subsequent liquor sale by Ryshavy.

assertion: In 1928 the Eighth Circuit affirmed an order barring use of the premises for one year from April 11, 1927.
locators: S83, Printed p. 38, opening paragraph describing the decree, and p. 39, reasoning and disposition.
supportExplanation: The opinion states the original order’s starting date and duration, explains why the tenant change did not establish abatement and affirms the decree.
qualification: The decision concerns the property under the National Prohibition Act’s civil nuisance provisions.

assertion: The postal circular records four pouches taken from a mail car in the Garrettsville robbery.
locators: S84, Paragraph beginning “A circular issued by the Post Office Department”
supportExplanation: The FBI case file reproduces the circular with the date, location and pouch count.
qualification: The circular’s account establishes the reported inventory. The early reports differ on the total number of robbers and the train number.

assertion: A postal inspector recorded the Plymouth’s specifications and key number and named Karpis and Campbell as suspects.
locators: S84, December 16, 1935, inspector interview on Plymouth details and suspects | S10, Printed p. 51, Garrettsville robbery and the identification of Bremer fugitives
supportExplanation: The December interview gives the car description and the inspectors’ suspicions. The later case summary identifies the two men as Bremer fugitives.
qualification: The FBI report documents the information supplied by the inspector. The key number is a detail of the description, with no proof it was the clue that identified the robbers.

assertion: The 1936 FBI summary identifies two fugitives from the Saint Paul Bremer case as participants in the Ohio mail robbery.
locators: S10, Printed p. 51, paragraph on identification of fugitives wanted in the Bremer kidnapping
supportExplanation: The case summary explicitly links the Garrettsville participants to the Bremer fugitive investigation.
qualification: The summary describes an investigative identification. It does not establish either man’s conviction for the train robbery.

assertion: Police sought entry to a licensed beer parlor on West Wheelock Parkway during the city’s Sunday closing hours.
locators: S85, pp. 208–209, opening paragraph and Ordinance No. 7641, section 1
supportExplanation: The court gives the date, address, time, officers’ observations outside, and ordinance hours.
qualification: The setting and timing come from the opinion’s account of the trial. The case concerned closing hours at a licensed business.

assertion: Officers reported seven partly filled beer glasses in front of two people and four men hiding in the basement.
locators: S85, p. 209, passage beginning with the officers’ admission after a delay
supportExplanation: The published opinion lists what the officers reported seeing at the bar, in the booth, in the basement, and in back.
qualification: The opinion summarizes police testimony. It leaves the building’s floor plan and the identity of the people in the booth unspecified.

assertion: The owners gave a surprise-planning explanation and the Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the after-hours convictions.
locators: S85, pp. 209–210, defendants’ testimony and final ruling
supportExplanation: The opinion sets out the owners’ account, ordinance, reasoning, and disposition.
qualification: The surprise was the defense’s explanation. The court ruled on after-hours business. The record establishes no gang connection.

assertion: Federal agents inventoried pencil-captioned childhood photographs and a picture described as Dillinger in naval uniform at the Lexington Avenue apartment.
locators: S76, Saint Paul file 26-2434, after printed p. 11 marker, paragraphs describing photographs of the boy in a cherry tree and wagon and Dillinger in naval uniform.
supportExplanation: The field report describes the photographs and reproduces the wording it records on their backs.
qualification: The age and identity of the boy in the tree come from the pencil caption recorded by agents. The inventory does not name the writer.

assertion: Agents reported that a road chart from the apartment ran from Newton National Bank to Saint Paul and sent it for laboratory examination.
locators: S76, Saint Paul file 26-2434, printed pp. 10–11 markers, paragraph beginning “In connection with the getaway road chart.”
supportExplanation: The field report gives the two ends of the chart, the agent who traced it and the laboratory referral.
qualification: The proposed getaway purpose was the investigators’ interpretation. This passage gives no evidence the route was used or that anyone robbed the bank.

assertion: The field report records Mrs. Coffey’s account of finding a telegram fragment under the carpet and transcribes the fragment.
locators: S76, Saint Paul file 26-2434, two paragraphs immediately before the printed p. 16 marker, Mrs. Coffey’s Western Union telegram fragment.
supportExplanation: Agents record that Coffey supplied the portion after the apartment inventory and quote its remaining text.
qualification: The location comes from Coffey. The cited passage does not establish who put the fragment there or what the message meant.

assertion: The appellate opinion records an initial $6,193.30 bill of costs against Gleckman, including juror meals, lodging and doctors’ services among about $2,500 in disputed tribunal expenses.
locators: S04, Reporter pp. 402–403, “On Taxation of Costs,” opening and assignment of error 18
supportExplanation: The costs section gives the clerk’s total and the expenses challenged under assignment of error 18.
qualification: The opinion gives a combined figure for the disputed group. It does not give the doctor’s charge by itself or describe the treatment.

assertion: The opinion records the $365.38 entry for Malone, explains why he did not testify, and directs that the costs of his attendance be limited to necessary travel and subsistence.
locators: S04, Reporter pp. 403–404, “Witness Michael F. Malone,” assignment of error 19 and the court’s answers
supportExplanation: The subsection on Malone itemizes the initial fees and mileage, explains the agreement about testimony, and states the governing rule.
qualification: The opinion establishes how to recalculate this item. It gives no final amount for Malone.

assertion: The appeals court affirmed Gleckman’s convictions and separately reversed the order on costs, directing removal of tribunal expenses and recalculation.
locators: S04, Reporter pp. 402–404, disposition on the merits, elimination of tribunal expenses, and final order on costs
supportExplanation: The merits decision affirms the judgment. The costs ruling directs removal of the listed expenses and ends by sending back the order for recalculation.
qualification: The opinion gives the directions on costs. The revised total is outside this record.

assertion: Saint Paul investigators recorded Bremer’s account of an overlapping whistle and siren and reported that the towns he visited with agents did not match his timing.
locators: S86, June 12, 1934 letter from Saint Paul, file 7-30, document p. 2 between archive stamps 305 and 306, paragraph beginning “Recent conferences with Mr. Bremer” | S87, June 7, 1934 R. E. Newby report, Saint Paul file 7-30, synopsis immediately after archive-stamped p. 720
supportExplanation: The June 12 letter gives the order of the sounds. Newby’s June 7 report describes the field trip and its result.
qualification: The pattern is Bremer’s recollection. The field report describes the resemblance of a bell rather than identifying the original bell.

assertion: A Saint Paul letter describes replies about church bells and sirens, and a field report records a Brookfield pastor’s account of 48 tolls to mark a parishioner’s death and age.
locators: S86, June 12, 1934 letter, first page above archive-stamped p. 305, discussion of lists and replies from clergy and officials | S88, Charles Jenkins report, March 14, 1934, “AT BROOKFIELD, ILLINOIS,” January 1934 table and the paragraph immediately below it
supportExplanation: The June 12 correspondence gives the categories of replies and how towns were sorted. The March 14 report records the Brookfield interview after Rockoff wrote to the Saint Paul office.
qualification: The bureau summarized how some recipients interpreted its questions. The Brookfield report records Rockoff’s account of his church bell without identifying it as the one Bremer heard.

assertion: D. M. Ladd requested permission to destroy the sound inquiry circulars after the hideout was found, and J. Edgar Hoover authorized it.
locators: S89, Bureau file 7-576-5763, April 29, 1935 letter from Ladd and immediately following May 7, 1935 reply from Hoover
supportExplanation: Ladd’s April 29 request and Hoover’s May 7 reply survive together in the case file.
qualification: The exchange establishes permission. It leaves the date and extent of any destruction open and does not show that the sound inquiry located the hideout.

assertion: An August 14 United Press dispatch reported that headlights drew investigators to the Wildwood shooting scene while they were checking a tip about Bugs Moran.
locators: S90, Printed p. 1, Saint Paul dateline, report beneath 'Trio Believed Slain By Rival Gangster Band'. | S91, Printed p. 1, Saint Paul dateline at start of 'Guns Take Five Lives.'
supportExplanation: The front-page dispatch gives the dateline, the location, the search for Moran, and the burning headlights. The Associated Press independently reports the three deaths near Wildwood.
qualification: The dispatch explains what reportedly brought officers to the area. Moran's role in the shooting remains unestablished.

assertion: The United Press continuation describes a gold basketball with the inscription 'K. C. ’20' as one of the items police used to identify Frank Coleman.
locators: S90, Printed p. 2, 'Trio Believed— (Continued from page 1),' paragraph beginning 'A gold basketball.'
supportExplanation: The continuation names Coleman, describes the token and chain, and associates them with the police identification.
qualification: The surviving dispatch gives no maker, photograph, or confirmed explanation of the inscription.

assertion: The August 14 wire dispatches give a tentative Saint Paul identification for the third man and report a police theory involving slot machine concessions.
locators: S90, Printed p. 1, tentative names below 'Trio Believed Slain By Rival Gangster Band.' | S91, Printed p. 1, 'Guns Take Five Lives,' Saint Paul dateline and 'Killed By Rivals' paragraphs.
supportExplanation: United Press identifies the third man tentatively as 'Butch' Myers. The Associated Press attributes the identification and the slot concession theory to police.
qualification: The contemporary reports preserve the early identification and motive theory. The third man's legal name and the shooters remain unresolved in these records.

assertion: Mr. Parnell told federal investigators that he saw suitcases being moved from the Grand Avenue apartments and a man turn with a revolver after a door squeaked.
locators: S82, Archive stamp 323 and following passage, Parnell’s March 3 or 4 account from the basketball game through the laundry-room door.
supportExplanation: The file records the basketball game, the call to police, Parnell’s laundry-room vantage and the squeaking door.
qualification: Parnell was recounting what he remembered. A later resemblance to a photograph of Arthur Barker did not establish the gunman’s identity.

assertion: The Parnells described a pickup of dishes and silverware authorized by a penciled note. Federal agents recorded sending the note for comparison.
locators: S82, Passage leading up to archive stamp 330, April 26 mover and pencil note, plus photo comparison and car registration passages before the Talbott interview. | S92, Report passage citing O. G. Hall’s March 7, 1934 report, printed pp. 4–5 and the following passage, departure, mover, and limits of photographic identification. | S81, February 26, 1934 Saint Paul letter, document p. 2 immediately after archive-stamped p. 52, paragraph beginning “The letter addressed to Mr. Coy O. Hardwick”
supportExplanation: The interviews and later case summary describe the pickup and the limits of photographic identification. The February 26 letter records sending the note and a separate letter to the director for comparison.
qualification: The reports give variants of the initials on the note and differ on which Parnell made the handoff. The photo resemblances did not settle the tenants’ identities.

assertion: A Bremer case memo records three Grand Avenue utility deposits, two returned checks, one check not returned, and signature tracings retained in Saint Paul.
locators: S93, PDF p. 13, R. L. Nalls’s March 19, 1934 Northern States Power Company memo, in the report stamped 7-576-1384.
supportExplanation: The report reproduces the utility inquiry, the different refund statuses and the agent’s account of keeping the tracings.
qualification: The memo records what the utility showed. It does not establish who received or cashed the third check or whose names the occupants were using.

assertion: The Associated Press reported that Haskell Bohn testified in Saint Paul and named Verne Sankey and Ray Robinson as his abductors.
locators: S94, June 12 Saint Paul dateline, ‘Testimony Opens in Case Involving Bohn Kidnaping’. | S95, January 3 Saint Paul dateline, paragraph following Kinkead’s statement about the athletes.
supportExplanation: The June 12 dateline names the first witness, describes the kidnapping, and reports Robinson’s plea and the ongoing search for Verne Sankey.
qualification: The dispatch reports testimony from the opening of Fern Sankey’s trial. Fern was acquitted, as the January 1934 dispatch later reported.

assertion: Kinkead reportedly described a file on Dempsey’s and Ruth’s earnings and a photograph of Ruth, and inferred a possible kidnapping scheme.
locators: S95, January 3 Saint Paul dateline, report on Kinkead’s suspicion about Sankey, paragraph beginning ‘We found in the basement’.
supportExplanation: The January 3 Saint Paul dispatch gives Kinkead’s account of the ranch search and quotes his description of the earnings file and Ruth picture.
qualification: The newspaper reports Kinkead’s description and inference. The original papers, author of the notation, and evidence of an actual attempt remain unlocated.

assertion: Contemporary reports attribute to Purvis an account of Sankey’s arrest and admissions in the Bohn and Denver cases, while continuing to attribute the athletes story to Kinkead.
locators: S96, ‘No Sankey Link to Lindbergh Case,’ continuation from first page, February 1 Chicago dateline through the paragraph beginning ‘The prosecutor also accused Sankey’.
supportExplanation: The February 1 dispatch records the barber-shop arrest and separately attributes the admissions and athlete allegation to the officials who described them.
qualification: The press gives Purvis’s account of the admissions. The athlete scheme remains Kinkead’s allegation.

assertion: The Saint Paul bureau’s June 16 letter records a jail-note route between Barker and Kuhlman and says the sheriff arranged for copies to reach the bureau before delivery.
locators: S97, June 16, 1935 letter, document p. 1, paragraph beginning “During the time that Arthur R. Barker was held”.
supportExplanation: Andersen names the guard, the two correspondents, the sheriff, and the order of copying and delivery.
qualification: The letter describes the arrangement for messages Hession handled. It gives no full inventory of the correspondence.

assertion: Hession told the Saint Paul bureau that he stayed at the Frederic Hotel under the name Ben Franklin and used the stay to handle the correspondence.
locators: S97, June 16, 1935 letter, document p. 1, Hession’s explanation beginning after the room and telephone charges.
supportExplanation: The letter records the name, dates, purpose and Hession’s account of his contact with Kuhlman.
qualification: The source summarizes Hession’s explanation. It does not reproduce the hotel register or independently establish what Barker or Kuhlman knew.

assertion: The June 16 letter itemizes Hession’s expense request and asks whether the bureau could cover it.
locators: S97, June 16, 1935 letter, document pp. 1–2, the $26.50 total, Chicago call, transfer to Leavenworth and reimbursement question.
supportExplanation: The first sheet records the total and the room charge. The continuation gives Hession’s explanation and asks about reimbursement.
qualification: The letter documents the request. The final payment disposition is unclear in this copy.
