assertion: The Associated Press reported that Touhy and three co-defendants arrived in Saint Paul in a special car attached to a mail train and were escorted off in handcuffed pairs.
locators: S98, Printed p. 6, August 19 Saint Paul dateline and the paragraphs on the arrival and transfer.
supportExplanation: The August 19 Saint Paul dateline gives the train, arrival time, handcuff pairings and armed escort to jail.
qualification: The wire report describes the transfer. The four were awaiting trial on the federal Hamm charges.

assertion: A contemporary dispatch places the September 25 hearing in a machine gun guarded courtroom in the jail basement and reports the judges kept bail at $100,000 each.
locators: S100, Printed p. 3, “Touhy Denied Bail Reduction,” September 25 Saint Paul dateline and last paragraph on the basement courtroom.
supportExplanation: The September 25 Saint Paul dispatch explains why the judges left their regular courtrooms and gives the motions, bail and the defendants’ route from their cells.
qualification: The account describes a hearing on motions before trial, with the judges' location reported as a security measure.

assertion: Contemporary dispatches describe armed security on the trial’s opening day and report that the jury acquitted all four defendants in the Hamm case.
locators: S101, Printed p. 1, “Armed Guards Circle Room at St. Paul,” opening Saint Paul dateline and “Curious Turned Back” paragraphs. | S102, Printed p. 1, “Fail to Convict Touhy Gangsters,” November 28 Saint Paul dateline, acquittal and description of the two charges.
supportExplanation: The November 9 story describes the tear gas guns and courthouse passes. The November 28 dispatch names the two federal charges and records the acquittals.
qualification: The November 28 verdict concerned the federal Hamm charges. The press reported separate Chicago charges in the John Factor case.

assertion: A February 26 Saint Paul memo specifies three sample lines, similar paper, and a 1929 portable Corona with pica type as the target.
locators: S81, February 26, 1934 Saint Paul typewriter memorandum, archive-stamped pp. 107–108, sample lines and laboratory description.
supportExplanation: The Saint Paul memo specifies the test and gives the laboratory’s description of the machine sought.
qualification: These were proposed test lines. The memo does not identify the machine that typed the ransom notes.

assertion: Agents found two records of the type of machine sought among roughly 500 repair slips and described the purple-ribbon Corona as an unlikely match.
locators: S82, J. E. Brennan’s “Re: Typewriters” memorandum, preceding archive stamp 320, eight months of slips and two machine entries. | S81, February 26, 1934 Saint Paul typewriter memorandum, archive-stamped p. 108, serial 656647, ribbon and assessment.
supportExplanation: Brennan’s memorandum describes the repair search and lists the machines. The February 26 memorandum describes the former purple ribbon on the second machine and records the agent’s assessment.
qualification: The repair slips identified candidates. The records cited here give no laboratory match to the notes.

assertion: Bureau correspondence documents the recovery of an Underwood, its detour to a supply shelf, missing routing labels, and the tentative identification of the ransom-note machine as a Corona.
locators: S103, R. E. Newby’s September 27, 1934 memorandum for Mr. Tamm and October 2, 1934 letter to the Detroit office, archive-stamped pp. 239–241.
supportExplanation: Newby’s September memorandum records the clerk’s discovery and the lab’s assessment. The October letter attributes the delay to the missing laboratory labels.
qualification: The September memo proposed a fingerprint check. These passages give no result for it and no confirmed identification of the ransom-note machine.

assertion: On July 13, 1932, the Manchester Evening Herald printed an Associated Press dispatch relaying the New York Sun’s claim that Abe Wagner had been killed about two months earlier and sunk in the East River in a barrel of cement.
locators: S104, July 13, 1932 issue, p. 2, ‘Abie Wagner Slain’
supportExplanation: The original newspaper page preserves the headline, attribution, time estimate and river name.
qualification: The dispatch establishes what reached print. The Saint Paul case contradicts the reported time and place of death.

assertion: Anne E. Cowie dates Wagner’s shooting near Snelling and University avenues in Saint Paul to July 25, 1932 and describes his fruit peddler cover.
locators: S105, Printed p. 12, paragraph beginning ‘Ramsey County’s national reputation,’ immediately before ‘Top Legal Talent’ | S106, July 22, 1933 letter, file 62-4949, p. 2, paragraph beginning ‘The St. Paul Office will observe’
supportExplanation: Cowie supplies the date, intersection and occupation. The July 1933 bureau letter records the Saint Paul arrests for the killing.
qualification: The date, intersection and fruit seller cover come from Cowie’s later account. A federal letter separately places the killing and arrests in Saint Paul.

assertion: Cowie’s county history records two convictions and life sentences in the Wagner case. A 1933 bureau letter uses different names for the two men and reports their July 26, 1932 arrests in Saint Paul for the murder of Abe Wagner.
locators: S105, Printed p. 12, ‘Top Legal Talent’ and the paragraph immediately preceding it | S106, July 22, 1933 letter, file 62-4949, p. 2, paragraph beginning ‘The St. Paul Office will observe’
supportExplanation: Cowie’s account names George Young and Joseph Schaefer and describes the conviction and sentence. Cullen lists Albert L. Silverburg and John Newman and names the victim Abe Wagner.
qualification: The federal letter was a summary written a year later. The compared passages leave the pairwise alias mapping and the method of identifying Wagner open.

assertion: The October 8 Associated Press dispatch identified Rutman as a dress shop proprietor and reported that he returned home after being held near White Bear Lake.
locators: S107, Printed p. 1, “Kidnaped Man Beaten Before Being Released,” October 8 Saint Paul dateline.
supportExplanation: The Pampa Daily News printed a Saint Paul dispatch describing Rutman’s occupation, release and hospitalization.
qualification: The release and hospital visit are reported in a contemporary dispatch. The cottage location comes from the account available at the time.

assertion: A later history identifies Rutman as a bootlegger and attributes his abduction to Jack Ferrick and associates, naming the Silver Slipper as the place he was held.
locators: S105, Printed p. 12, paragraph naming Morris Rutman, Jack Ferrick and the Silver Slipper. See note 25 for the citation to Paul Maccabee.
supportExplanation: The historical account gives the Saint Paul abduction, names Ferrick and places Rutman at the Silver Slipper in Mahtomedi.
qualification: The names and venue come from Cowie’s later account, which cites Paul Maccabee. The early wire gave a general location near White Bear Lake.

assertion: The contemporary press attributed the $50,000 demand to Rutman and carried conflicting reports about whether a payment followed.
locators: S107, Printed p. 1, “Kidnaped Man Beaten Before Being Released,” October 8 Saint Paul dateline, closing sentence on the demand. | S108, October 8 Saint Paul dateline, paragraphs between the demand and the “Was Abducted” subhead.
supportExplanation: The short dispatch records the amount Rutman said was demanded. The longer dispatch records the denial and the friends’ report that relatives paid.
qualification: The amount is the reported demand. The longer report’s police denial and secondhand report from friends leave the outcome unresolved.

assertion: The federal case file records that the man who encountered officers at Lincoln Court presented himself as a soap salesman.
locators: S41, April 8, 1934 memorandum for the Director, first page, about 2 p.m. call with Clegg and paragraphs on the soap salesman. | S11, “The Bureau Actively Joins the Hunt,” March 31 Lincoln Court encounter and flight.
supportExplanation: The memo records the cover story as investigators discussed the man’s identity. The agency’s later narrative describes the corresponding encounter.
qualification: The later FBI case history identifies Van Meter and describes the armed encounter. The contemporary April 8 memo records uncertainty about his identification.

assertion: The April 8 memorandum records Coulter’s tentative identification, facial resemblance to Green, and the lack of a fingerprint finding at that point.
locators: S41, April 8, 1934 memorandum for the Director, first page, paragraph beginning “I asked him if we had enough information on Van Meter.”
supportExplanation: The writer summarizes an afternoon call with Clegg in which the officers discussed Van Meter as a possible identification.
qualification: This is a record of what the investigators knew on April 8. It gives no later fingerprint result.

assertion: Skinner said Van Meter told her he was the man who used the soap-sales story and fired at an officer, and the FBI’s later history identifies Van Meter at the scene.
locators: S41, Interview of Bessie Skinner, printed p. 10, paragraph beginning “She stated that to her knowledge Homer Van Meter” and continuing into the alleged admission. | S11, “The Bureau Actively Joins the Hunt,” March 31 Lincoln Court encounter.
supportExplanation: Clegg’s interview write-up records Skinner’s account of Van Meter’s statement. The FBI case history names him in its account of the hallway encounter.
qualification: Skinner was reporting a later conversation. She did not witness the encounter at Lincoln Court.

assertion: Gold’s history says the owner of a missing Buick roadster valued at $1,400 spotted it at a garage while riding a streetcar near University and Dale in Saint Paul.
locators: S36, Printed p. 14, ‘The Car Thief,’ first paragraph
supportExplanation: The first paragraph of ‘The Car Thief’ gives the model, value, streetcar and intersection.
qualification: The sighting and valuation are from Gold’s retrospective account.

assertion: Gold says the owner found brochures from his nut-shelling plant in the Buick, called police, and that Taran appeared before Judge Hugo Hanft on a car theft charge.
locators: S36, Printed p. 14, ‘The Car Thief,’ first two paragraphs, and adjacent ‘The Bootlegger’ section
supportExplanation: Gold describes the discovery and the phone call, then recounts Taran’s court appearance. The surrounding article establishes Taran’s boxing and later bootlegging history.
qualification: The source describes the brochures and the charge. The brochures themselves are unavailable and the charge does not establish that Taran stole the Buick.

assertion: Gold reports that Taran was released and quotes the St. Paul Daily News reporting Judge Hanft’s advice to stick to tailoring.
locators: S36, Printed p. 14, ‘The Car Thief,’ second paragraph, including the St. Paul Daily News quotation
supportExplanation: Gold reports the release and quotes the contemporary newspaper’s description of the advice.
qualification: The newspaper sentence survives here as quoted by Gold. Gold gives no original docket or later disposition for this charge.

assertion: A contemporary dispatch reports Hogan’s death after surgery on December 4, 1928. A later account reports that people including a boxing champion offered to donate blood at the hospital.
locators: S109, Front page, ‘Underworld Leader Dies From Injuries,’ December 4 Saint Paul dateline. | S110, Opening paragraph and paragraph about the amputation and blood-transfusion offers.
supportExplanation: The AP’s two-paragraph item records the fatal bombing and amputation. Curt Brown’s opening and his account of the surgery describe the people who volunteered.
qualification: The later account describes offers to donate. The available reporting leaves the identities and participation of individual donors unconfirmed.

assertion: Contemporary local coverage tied Hogan’s death to a prediction of fewer Christmas turkey dinners in Saint Paul.
locators: S110, Paragraph beginning ‘He was the idol of not a few persons,’ followed by the Christmas dinner line. | S111, Significance narrative, sections 9–end p. 35, ‘Dapper Dan’ Hogan paragraph and note 45.
supportExplanation: Brown reproduces the line from the Minneapolis Morning Tribune. The Calvary Cemetery registration form cites the December 5 front-page death story by title.
qualification: The line is the 1928 newspaper’s characterization, as quoted by Curt Brown in 2018. It gives the paper’s view of Hogan’s reputation among some people.

assertion: A local history describes more than 2,000 mourners and five carloads of flowers at Hogan’s funeral, and recounts a witness remembering Granada Club regulars in the church.
locators: S112, Printed p. 9, paragraph immediately before ‘Epilogue.’
supportExplanation: The last two paragraphs before the epilogue give the crowd estimate, the flowers and the recollection inside the church.
qualification: The turnout and flowers are estimates from a later account. The recollection of club regulars is attributed to Harry Turgeon.

assertion: A June 17 United Press report described the two ransom-related notes, the taxi driver’s arrest at the Dunn home, and his account of being paid $2 for the delivery.
locators: S113, June 17, 1933, front page, Saint Paul dateline under ‘William Hamm Is Held’; paragraphs from the delivery to Dunn’s home through the photograph of Sankey.
supportExplanation: The dispatch recounts the delivery and arrest, then attributes the fee and explanation to the driver.
qualification: The dispatch reports what the driver said about the fee and his knowledge of the notes.

assertion: The June dispatch reported a tentative reaction to Sankey’s photograph, while the description for press photograph 97 identifies Allison and records that he described a resemblance to McFadden.
locators: S113, June 17, 1933, front page, paragraph describing the driver’s reaction to the photograph of Verne Sankey. | S114, Crime Photographs collection, item 97, ‘Hamm, William A. Jr. 1933.’
supportExplanation: United Press records the suspicion about the Sankey photo. Kent State identifies Allison and summarizes his response about McFadden at trial.
qualification: The June item is a wire report. The archive entry is a photograph description and supplies no verbatim transcript.

assertion: The November 28 Associated Press dispatch reported that a federal jury acquitted McFadden, Touhy, Sharkey and Schaefer on both Hamm kidnapping counts.
locators: S102, November 28, 1933, front page, ‘Fail to Convict Touhy Gangsters,’ opening paragraphs and description of counts.
supportExplanation: The dispatch gives all four defendants’ names, the acquittal, and the two counts in the Hamm case.
qualification: The article reports the verdict and charges and supplies no jury deliberations.

assertion: Cherrington told agents that she, her sister and Hamilton contacted Van Meter at a Saint Paul restaurant and stayed four days at a cottage she identified as Harry Sawyer’s before a warning prompted their return.
locators: S115, Bremer Kidnapping Part 145, opening page, paragraph beginning ‘PATRICIA CHERRINGTON,’ immediately before the Vivian Mathias paragraph.
supportExplanation: The report attributes the restaurant, Van Meter’s role, the four-day stay and the warning to Cherrington.
qualification: The file summarizes Cherrington’s account. It gives neither the restaurant’s name nor the cottage’s address.

assertion: Skinner told agents that she had heard from Van Meter about the trio’s route to McCormick’s restaurant and their departure in a Ford, and she gave her belief about the destination.
locators: S116, Bremer Kidnapping Part 175, Bessie Skinner interview, paragraph beginning ‘According to information Mrs. Skinner received from Van Meter on the day of the shooting on Lexington Avenue’.
supportExplanation: The interview specifies the named restaurant, vehicle, and Skinner’s stated basis for the account.
qualification: Skinner’s route is secondhand, and she described the farm as her belief.

assertion: A federal witness outline attributed to Werner Hanni the discovery of a light tan woman’s coat with a platinum fox collar and Young-Quinlan label in Apartment 303 at Lincoln Court.
locators: S41, Dillinger Gang Part 12, witness outline near the end of the volume, after printed p. 5 marker, Werner Hanni entry, paragraph beginning ‘Witness will further testify that among the effects’.
supportExplanation: Hanni’s witness entry gives the apartment number and the coat’s appearance and label.
qualification: The outline describes expected testimony and names no purchaser or owner for the coat.

assertion: The FBI witness outline and trial summary both say Bremer discarded the goggles in weeds after the kidnappers drove away, but record different instructions about how high to count.
locators: S117, P. 018, Edward G. Bremer outline, final Rochester roadside paragraph. | S119, Printed p. 5, summary of Bremer’s release testimony. | S118, P. 059, Glynn outline, recovery on or about February 17, 1934.
supportExplanation: The witness outline records fifteen and a restart at five. The later summary records ten and confirms Bremer’s account of discarding the goggles.
qualification: These are an outline and an agent’s trial summary, not verbatim testimony. The trial summary also misdates the release to 1935; the recovery outline places the recovery in February 1934.

assertion: Glynn’s FBI witness outline says he found Bremer’s discarded goggles under about three inches of snow in Rochester and sent them to the Saint Paul office.
locators: S118, P. 059, Special Agent M. P. Glynn witness outline.
supportExplanation: The outline names Glynn and Rhode, describes the gap behind the building and states that Glynn sent the goggles to the Saint Paul office.
qualification: The location and snow depth are recorded in the Bureau’s outline of Glynn’s expected testimony; they are not modern site measurements.

assertion: The FBI’s trial preparation file listed the welder’s goggles in Bureau custody and said they would go to the U.S. attorney in Saint Paul for Bremer to identify.
locators: S117, Archive stamp 649, Items to Be Identified by Victim Bremer, Goggles entry.
supportExplanation: The Goggles entry states who had the item, where it was to be sent, and who could identify it.
qualification: The list gives the planned transfer and identification. It does not establish admission as an exhibit or the goggles’ current whereabouts.

assertion: Hoover’s April 30 memorandum says an Uptown State Bank cashier matched serial numbers to the Bremer ransom, and a subsequent report from First National Bank led agents to William Vidler.
locators: S120, April 30, 1934 memorandum for the Attorney General, first sheet, paragraphs beginning ‘On April 23’ and ‘On April 26’
supportExplanation: The memo’s first paragraph describes the cashier’s match and the circular. Its second describes the First National Bank exchange and the arrest.
qualification: The memo gives the Bureau’s contemporary account of the bank employees’ actions. It describes the ransom match for some bills and leaves the provenance of the rest open.

assertion: A field report describes Jack McLaughlin trying on the wrong hat before agents found two envelopes under the sweatband of the hat he next identified. The field report and Hoover’s memo both report a match to Bremer ransom bills.
locators: S120, Chicago field narrative, printed pp. 48–49, search of Rack No. 17 and examination of the brown felt hat; passage after McLaughlin’s signed statement, search ‘ransom list’; April 30, 1934 Attorney General memo, first sheet
supportExplanation: The field report describes the gray and brown hats, the envelopes and the comparison to the ransom list. Hoover’s memo separately reports that some of the cash was identified as ransom.
qualification: The field report records the agents’ version of the encounter. The field report and Hoover’s memo give different amounts for cash recovered and linked to the ransom.

assertion: The June 1934 correspondence records Vidler’s request for $460, the Saint Paul prosecutor’s decision to make no evidentiary claim to the sum, and Purvis’s proposed handling of the seal. A jury later acquitted Vidler and convicted John J. McLaughlin Sr. in the Saint Paul criminal case.
locators: S121, June 25 Sullivan and June 26 Purvis letters, archive-stamped pp. 186–188; Vidler petition in the Northern District of Illinois, stamps 233–235 | S10, Printed pp. 44–45, April 15 opening of the Saint Paul trial and May 17, 1935 verdicts
supportExplanation: Sullivan’s June 25 letter and Purvis’s June 26 letter name the sum and give each office’s position. The later Bremer investigation summary lists the May 17, 1935 verdicts.
qualification: The petition and correspondence describe a requested return. They give no final ruling about the cash. The acquittal is the verdict in the criminal case.

assertion: Arthur Murray’s witness outline records a package left at the New Hotel Brunswick by a man who said his father needed medicine and had missed the bus.
locators: S117, P. 043, Arthur Murray witness outline.
supportExplanation: The FBI outline names the hotel and recounts both visits and the explanation given for holding the package.
qualification: The outline records what Murray said he was told. It does not identify the messenger or establish that the father or illness was real.

assertion: The Murray witness outlines say a Bremer ransom note found in an unclaimed cornmeal box directed its recipient to a marked black Chevrolet in Owatonna.
locators: S117, Pp. 043–044, Arthur Murray and Mrs. George M. Murray witness outlines.
supportExplanation: Arthur Murray’s outline gives the delay. The outline for his mother describes opening the package and transcribes the directions.
qualification: The directions are transcribed in the witness outline. Their presence in the note does not establish that the car was there or that a payoff man followed them.

assertion: George M. Murray’s outline says he forwarded the note to the state Bureau of Criminal Apprehension in Saint Paul on March 31, 1934; the Bureau planned to send the cornmeal box to the U.S. attorney.
locators: S117, Pp. 043–045, Arthur and George M. Murray witness outlines; p. 018, Edward Bremer release account.
supportExplanation: George Murray’s outline dates the forwarding, while Arthur Murray’s page records the intended transfer of the cornmeal box and places delivery before the release.
qualification: The file records the reported forwarding of the note and an intended transfer of the box, with no proof that the box was admitted in court.

assertion: A 1935 Associated Press dispatch described a siren and smoke at the 1933 South Saint Paul payroll robbery, the shooting of officers Pavlak and Yeaman, and Stassen’s announcement connecting the car to a Chicago robbery.
locators: S122, March 12, 1935, Fairmont Daily Sentinel, South Saint Paul dateline, ‘Machine Gun Used Stolen From Police’ and continuation under ‘Auto Also Identified’.
supportExplanation: The South Saint Paul dateline gives the date, deaths and injuries, and the continuation describes the smoke, siren and vehicle link.
qualification: The dispatch recounts the 1933 robbery and reports what the county attorney announced in 1935.

assertion: A July 29, 1935 federal report identified the Hudson abandoned in Chicago as a black 1933 sedan and described its siren, smoke-screen equipment, bullet-resistant glass and steel armor.
locators: S123, D. P. Sullivan’s July 29, 1935 report, printed pp. 9–12, Chicago robbery, abandoned Hudson and equipment paragraph immediately after the plate checks.
supportExplanation: The Chicago robbery summary describes the smoke screen and abandonment. The following pages identify the model and list the modifications and the auto body shop.
qualification: The report describes the equipment and records the investigators’ findings. It gives no complete diagram or operating description.

assertion: The July 29 federal report describes Florida plates on the recovered Hudson and says police linked Minnesota plates found inside, issued for a Duluth Ford, to the South Saint Paul robbery.
locators: S123, D. P. Sullivan’s July 29, 1935 report, printed pp. 11–12, Florida plate number, interior inventory and Minnesota B141186 registration check.
supportExplanation: The car inventory separates the mounted Florida plates from Minnesota sets recovered inside. The report then traces the Duluth Ford pair and describes its link to the earlier robbery.
qualification: The report attributes the identification to Chicago police files. It gives no exact mounting history for all the other plates.

assertion: Period newspaper and magazine accounts describe Wallace Jamie presenting himself as a student of police work or an efficiency expert while investigating Saint Paul police ties to the underworld, with microphones hidden in lamps.
locators: S124, August 16, 1935, p. 2, ‘He Stirred St. Paul’ | S125, July 1936, printed p. 53, opening account and caption beginning ‘Inside lamps’
supportExplanation: The August 1935 feature and July 1936 illustrated account both describe Jamie in the public safety building and mention microphones in lamps.
qualification: The magazine describes an efficiency survey. The newspaper says Jamie asked to observe police at work. Each account supplies different additional microphone locations.

assertion: Modern Mechanix reported that Jamie used a pamograph to cut conversations onto aluminum discs and adapted a fire alarm recorder to log telephone numbers dialed.
locators: S125, July 1936, printed p. 127, paragraphs beginning ‘The method of listening’ and ‘Ticker Tape Records Telephone Numbers’; p. 53 captions
supportExplanation: The continuation describes the pamograph, its sapphire needle and the fire alarm apparatus under ‘Ticker Tape Records Telephone Numbers.’
qualification: The illustrated account describes the two instruments and gives a hypothetical telephone number as an example. It reproduces no original call tape or conversation.

assertion: Modern Mechanix reported that a janitor found recording equipment in a ventilation shaft and that recordings went to city and county officials. Cowie’s county history links Jamie’s investigation to a 1935 grand jury inquiry and twenty-one indictments.
locators: S125, July 1936, printed p. 127, ‘Janitor Tips Off Jamie’s Plot’ | S105, Printed p. 13, paragraph beginning ‘In May, 1934, a young man named Wallace Ness Jamie’
supportExplanation: The magazine’s closing paragraphs give the discovery and recipients. Cowie’s history describes the subsequent grand jury and official discipline.
qualification: The janitor episode is from the magazine. The later county history supplies the count of indictments, which are formal charges.

assertion: The Associated Press reported that Antink identified Morrie Moll, also known as Morrie Miller, in Saint Paul. A later account places the meeting in the governor’s office.
locators: S126, Printed p. 1, September 27 Los Angeles dispatch, paragraph naming the Phantom Gunman and describing Antink’s identification in Saint Paul. | S128, Paragraph immediately after the ‘Moll arrested in Florida 2-6-1929’ caption, on the June 5 identification. | S45, 170 Minn. 197, paragraphs discussing the alleged liquor syndicate and Morrie Miller.
supportExplanation: The Eugene Guard’s September 27 Los Angeles dispatch names Moll’s alias and reports Antink’s Saint Paul identification. The Gleeman opinion records the brothers’ allegations about Morrie Miller, and Graham gives the date and place of Antink’s identification.
qualification: The contemporary dispatch places the identification in Saint Paul that spring. The office and June 5 date come from Graham’s later account.

assertion: Moll was reported released on $10,000 bail and the 1929 transfer to California failed. The available accounts give different versions of the warrant decision.
locators: S127, Printed p. 1, ‘Killed in Revenge for Foiling Crime,’ paragraph on bail and ‘Extradition Tried’ subheading. | S128, Paragraph beginning ‘The extradition to Los Angeles was granted on June 15.’
supportExplanation: The Albany Democrat-Herald carries the bail figure and Fitts’s account of a refusal. Graham reports approval on June 15 followed by release and disappearance.
qualification: The two accounts conflict over the warrant. The original extradition papers would be needed to resolve the decision and the chronology.

assertion: After Antink’s 1929 killing, the district attorney publicly blamed authorities for the failed transfer, police sought Moll, and the 1933 press reported that the killers had yet to be apprehended.
locators: S126, Printed p. 1, September 27 Los Angeles dispatch, Fitts’s statement and paragraphs on the police search. | S129, August 29 Hollywood dateline, story about a shooting in an Italian restaurant, paragraphs on David Antink and Morris Moll.
supportExplanation: The 1929 Associated Press report records the killing, Fitts’s statement and the police search. The August 29, 1933 dispatch says the people who killed Antink had yet to be apprehended.
qualification: The criticism and identification of a suspect are attributed to the officials who made them. The later dispatch records the status of the investigation in August 1933.

assertion: The Bureau put Doyle at Twin Oaks in Saint Paul in 1932, and a separate agent report placed him at 23 Warner Plaza under the name Stacey at the time of the January 1935 Saint Paul indictment. The federal charge against him was later dismissed.
locators: S89, Kansas City follow-up, p. 1, paragraph referring to the agent’s April 25, 1935 Bremer report, just before printed p. 2. | S10, Paragraph beginning ‘November 1932 to December 1932,’ Twin Oaks; printed pp. 44–45, January indictments and May 6 dismissal.
supportExplanation: The Bureau summary places Doyle at Twin Oaks and records the indictment and dismissal. The Kansas City agent report records the companion’s statement about Warner Plaza and the Stacey alias.
qualification: Doyle’s companion supplied the alias account. The Saint Paul kidnapping-conspiracy charge was dismissed.

assertion: The Kansas City telegram records a federal apartment search that omitted refrigerated food containers and attributes the janitor’s reported discovery in a can to local press coverage.
locators: S122, Western Union Kansas City telegram KA17 72, signed Nathan, beginning ‘BREKID LOCAL PRESS TODAY STATES BOND,’ March 20, 1935 stamp.
supportExplanation: The wire records the scope of the federal search in one passage and cites the local press for the janitor and the can in another.
qualification: The telegram describes the Bureau’s own search and repeats a press account of the find. It promises to verify the press account.

assertion: An FBI letter records a $1,000 Peabody bond, serial 56, recovered in Doyle’s apartment and identified by the Bank of Drexel cashier as stolen from his bank, despite Davis’s suggestion that it came from a mail robbery.
locators: S130, E. L. Conroy letter from Kansas City to Oklahoma City, September 1935, handwritten p. 67, citing R. P. Shanahan’s February 21 report on bond serial 56.
supportExplanation: Conroy’s letter gives the value and serial, names the bank and robbery date, and distinguishes Davis’s account from the cashier’s identification in Shanahan’s report.
qualification: The letter summarizes the cashier’s identification and Doyle’s reported admission. It does not describe the container or identify who put the bond there.

assertion: The federal outline of Byron Bolton’s expected testimony says he overheard a conversation about a Florida lake, a cottage and an alligator called Big Joe at a pecan ranch south of Macon. A longer interview records his account of a baited barrel and the alligator getting away.
locators: S118, Printed p. 110, Byron Bolton witness outline, paragraph beginning ‘BOLTON will further state’ and describing the pecan ranch. P. 111 identifies the underlying interview record in Saint Paul. | S131, Statement under the name Monte Carter, immediately before printed p. 105, paragraph on Big Joe and the bait.
supportExplanation: Bolton’s outline names the four men and records the conversation about the lake, hunting, the motorboat and the alligator. The interview under the name Monte Carter includes the barrel and what the men said happened.
qualification: The outline describes what Bolton said he overheard. It places the ranch about 30 to 50 miles south of Macon and gives no exact location. Bolton reports the bait story secondhand.

assertion: A February 1935 bureau memorandum records two Florida maps found in Doc Barker’s Chicago apartment and Bolton’s opinion that their marks pointed to the hideout.
locators: S122, February 8, 1935 memorandum for the director, p. 1, first three paragraphs and the January 11 interview. | S10, Printed pp. 38–39, paragraph on the Chicago search, marked map and alligator report.
supportExplanation: The memorandum’s opening gives the two marks separately and specifies that the maps were shown to Bolton before investigators went to Florida.
qualification: The memorandum records recovery of the maps. Bolton’s identification of the marks is his interpretation. The later summary describes a single map with a circle around Ocala and Lake Weir.

assertion: The bureau’s records describe how the marked maps and information about the alligator preceded the Florida inquiries that located Fred and Kate Barker at Lake Weir.
locators: S122, February 8, 1935 memorandum for the director, pp. 1–2, Florida investigation and identification of the cottage occupants. | S10, Printed pp. 38–39, marked map, Old Joe and the location of the Lake Weir cottage.
supportExplanation: The February memorandum records the dates and the inquiries near Ocala. The 1936 investigation summary identifies the Lake Weir cottage and gives the alligator nickname as Old Joe.
qualification: Both accounts come from the federal investigation. They record the agents’ search and do not establish that the alligator alone identified the cottage.

assertion: Frechette was convicted in Saint Paul of conspiring to harbor a fugitive. In July 1936 The Billboard reported that she had joined Scout Younger’s Arizona Dust Bowl carnival attraction.
locators: S11, The Bureau Actively Joins the Hunt, paragraph on Frechette’s Saint Paul trial and sentence. | S132, Printed p. 51, Dodson World’s Fair Shows, Johnstown dispatch by Dick Collins.
supportExplanation: The case history gives the location, charge and sentence. The trade report names Frechette, Younger and the attraction.
qualification: The FBI’s case history gives the conviction and sentence. The carnival dispatch identifies the booking without describing a performance or linking this attraction to the later show as the same production.

assertion: The January 9, 1937 Billboard item names Frechette as the feature of Crime Does Not Pay, lists people who worked on the show, and mentions several wax figures in a picture of the group.
locators: S133, Printed p. 50, Carnivals column, item opening ‘A recent picture on hand’.
supportExplanation: The item says the company was playing theaters and supplies a roster of the people and wax figures shown in the photograph.
qualification: The trade paper describes a photograph and names the people. It gives no names for the wax figures and leaves their role in the performance unclear.

assertion: On April 8, 1937, Camden chamber of commerce secretary Frank H. Heath wrote to Hoover about posters promising a personal appearance by Frechette and asked whether the performer could be her.
locators: S134, April 8, 1937 letter from Frank H. Heath to J. Edgar Hoover, first sheet after FOIA cover.
supportExplanation: Heath names the theater, describes where he saw the posters and asks Hoover to verify the advertised identity.
qualification: The letter records Heath’s suspicion. It leaves open whether the advertised Camden performance took place.

assertion: The FBI’s May 29, 1937 letter describes Frechette answering audience questions at a Pittsburgh carnival and says a Bureau stenographer who attended recognized her from office photographs.
locators: S134, May 29, 1937, letter from the Pittsburgh field office to the Director, file 62-47968-4.
supportExplanation: The letter names the act, describes the audience questions and gives the basis for identifying the performer.
qualification: The memo summarizes selected answers and records the stenographer’s identification in Pittsburgh. It gives no transcript and does not verify every booking or establish the facts of Frechette’s answers.

assertion: The indictment reproduced in Goldberg v. United States described three freight cars carrying whiskey beneath scrap iron from Winnipeg to Minneapolis before national Prohibition took effect.
locators: S135, 277 F. 211, pp. 213–215, paragraphs 26–27 on the indictment and the existing prohibition on imports.
supportExplanation: The decision reproduces the counts and dates in the indictment and explains that federal law had prohibited importation since 1917.
qualification: The identifiers, counts and siding dates are allegations reproduced in the appellate opinion. The court affirmed the convictions on appeal.

assertion: Quinn’s dissent describes a December 26 bank vault visit and railroad records putting the first car in Saint Paul on December 29 and Minneapolis on December 31.
locators: S136, 147 Minn. 383, p. 394, Quinn’s dissent, first numbered example of Weisman’s testimony.
supportExplanation: The dissent recounts Weisman’s testimony and uses the two record sets to challenge the timing.
qualification: Quinn treated the dates as a reason to reject Weisman’s account. The court’s controlling opinion applied a limited review of the governor’s decision.

assertion: A federal jury acquitted Nash, Governor Burnquist removed him after a hearing at the State Capitol, and the Minnesota Supreme Court left the order in place.
locators: S136, 147 Minn. 383, pp. 385, 387–392, hearing, findings, federal acquittal and disposition; Quinn dissent beginning p. 392. | S137, Paragraph beginning ‘Martinson admitted,’ account of Nash’s acquittal and the state Capitol removal hearing.
supportExplanation: The state opinion gives both outcomes and distinguishes the proceedings. MNopedia locates the governor’s hearing at the Capitol.
qualification: The acquittal was in the criminal case. The governor’s proceeding addressed fitness to hold office, and the court reviewed the removal under a limited standard.

assertion: The Minnesota Supreme Court records a disabled Lincoln in Como Park after the bank robbery, Peterson’s identification of Hankins as the man with a white sack, and Hankins’s first-degree murder conviction.
locators: S138, Printed pp. 375–377, ¶¶1–5, robbery, disabled Lincoln, and J. H. Peterson’s testimony.
supportExplanation: The opinion gives the date and police deaths, summarizes Peterson’s observation and identifies the conviction under review.
qualification: The sack and the identification come from Peterson’s testimony as summarized by the court. The passage does not give the contents of the sack.

assertion: The opinion describes aluminum grips and chiseled-off factory numbers on both pistols. A prosecution expert attributed the work on both to the same tool.
locators: S138, Printed p. 377, ¶¶6–7, weapons and tool marks; p. 379, ¶11, exhibit K.
supportExplanation: The court describes each arrest, identifies Exhibit K as the pistol found on Hankins and summarizes the prosecution expert’s comparison.
qualification: The same-tool comparison is the expert’s testimony as summarized in the opinion. The account leaves who altered the pistols and who fired each gun open.

assertion: The opinion describes Hankins’s account of obtaining the gun, the state’s rebuttal, and the barber’s alibi alongside Hankins’s own pretrial account. The court affirmed the denial of a new trial.
locators: S138, Printed pp. 379–382, ¶¶11–14 and ¶20, possession testimony, rebuttal, competing alibi and disposition.
supportExplanation: The opinion recounts Hankins’s testimony, witnesses who described his earlier possession of a similar gun, the Wabasha Street alibi, and Hankins’s own statement before affirming the order.
qualification: The opinion summarizes competing testimony and statements. Its ruling left the original conviction in place.

assertion: Touhy’s car struck a telephone pole near Elkhorn on July 19, 1933. A contemporary report identifies Harry Ward as the unarmed officer who stopped the men.
locators: S139, September 1, 1933, ‘Wisconsin News,’ Milwaukee item naming Harry Ward. | S140, 361 Ill. 332, paragraph beginning ‘Touhy, Stevens and McFadden filed a motion to suppress.’
supportExplanation: The Kewaskum Statesman places the four men at the crash and names Ward. The Illinois opinion supplies the date and describes the crash and seizure.
qualification: The newspaper names Ward and summarizes the arrests. The later opinion describes the crash and gun seizure in the separate John Factor prosecution.

assertion: Later accounts describe going to the jail over the pole damage. Touhy remembered $22.50, and the county recounts Sharkey riding a chicken truck to Lake Geneva and calling the jail.
locators: S141, Chapter 10, ‘Gone Fishing,’ paragraphs beginning ‘At the little town of Elkhorn’ and ‘I waited until a policeman.’ | S142, ‘Roger Touhy’ and ‘Arrest & Parole’ sections, paragraphs on the pole damage and Sharkey’s arrest.
supportExplanation: The memoir reports the price of replacing the pole. The county history gives Ward’s purpose and the account of Sharkey’s arrest.
qualification: The dollar amount and the chicken-truck detail come from separate later accounts. No bill or receipt was located.

assertion: Contemporary coverage printed a photograph of Touhy in Elkhorn custody, reported the four men’s transfer to Saint Paul on Hamm charges, and reported their federal acquittal in November.
locators: S143, July 22, 1933, front page, photograph and caption ‘First Photo of Roger Touhy, Chicago Gangster.’ | S139, ‘Wisconsin News,’ Milwaukee item, opening sentence on the Saint Paul transfer. | S102, Printed p. 1, ‘Fail to Convict Touhy Gangsters,’ November 28 Saint Paul dateline.
supportExplanation: The Manchester caption describes the deputies, photograph and crash. The Kewaskum item reports the Saint Paul transfer. The Medford dispatch gives the verdict.
qualification: The ‘first photo’ claim is the Herald’s caption. The verdict concerns the federal Hamm charges.

assertion: A Bureau memorandum says Austin was arrested at the conclusion of his January 20 Chicago wedding ceremony. A federal investigation summary identifies him as the Whitey named in the January 22 Saint Paul indictment.
locators: S144, April 15, 1935 memorandum in press-release form, p. 2, paragraph beginning ‘John J. McLaughlin, Sr., was located,’ enclosure 7-576-5572X. | S10, Printed pp. 44–45, the January 22, 1935 superseding indictments and identification of Whitey.
supportExplanation: The April 15 memorandum gives both names and dates the arrest. The November 1936 case summary identifies the alias in the conspiracy indictment.
qualification: The memo places the arrest at the end of the ceremony and gives no exact venue or sequence of events in the room. The indictment was a charge.

assertion: Shafetz recorded Mrs. Austin’s account of two calls answered by her mother and told her the Chicago Bureau had not made them.
locators: S145, Printed p. 88, passage beginning ‘The following investigation was conducted by Special Agent M. Shafetz on March 18, 1935’.
supportExplanation: The March 18 report gives the call date, the reported claim of federal authority, and Shafetz’s response in person.
qualification: Mrs. Austin did not speak to the callers. The report preserves her account of what her mother heard and the agent’s response, and gives no caller identity or motive.

assertion: The Bureau named Austin among the April 15 Saint Paul defendants and later recorded his May 6 discharge from custody and an October 11 murder conviction in Chicago.
locators: S144, April 15, 1935 memorandum, p. 1, defendant list, enclosure 7-576-5572X. | S10, Printed p. 45, paragraph beginning ‘Bruno Austin on May 6, 1935’.
supportExplanation: The April memo lists Austin as the trial opened. The November 1936 summary records the discharge, rearrest and Chicago sentence.
qualification: The Bureau summary gives the disposition of custody in Saint Paul and describes a separate murder case in Chicago.

assertion: The Bureau’s investigation summary describes Karpis and Campbell escaping the hotel during a gunfight that wounded Dolores Delaney. It names both men in the January 22 Saint Paul indictment.
locators: S10, Printed p. 41, Atlantic City garage and hotel escape; p. 44, January 22 kidnapping indictment naming Karpis and Campbell.
supportExplanation: The summary places the car in the Coast Garage and recounts the hallway encounter, escape and Delaney’s wound. Its later indictment section names both men in the Saint Paul case.
qualification: The summary describes the man in the hallway without naming him in that sentence. Its account gives no reason to assign that detail to either fugitive by name.

assertion: The January 21 AP dispatch reported the clothing-store alert, each man’s clothing, and the authorities’ belief that both fugitives remained in Atlantic City.
locators: S146, January 21, 1935, p. 1, Atlantic City AP dispatch, paragraphs on clothing stores, the bridges and the two descriptions.
supportExplanation: The AP story gives the warning, the guarded bridges and the garments it reports each man wore.
qualification: The dispatch reports the authorities’ belief and its account of the men’s clothing at the time.

assertion: The Bureau’s later investigation summary says the fugitives left Atlantic City in a stolen Pontiac and abandoned it near Quakertown, Pennsylvania.
locators: S10, Printed p. 41, paragraph beginning ‘After escaping from the hotel,’ Pontiac and Dr. Hunsicker. | S146, January 21, 1935, p. 1, paragraph reporting the police belief and guarded highway bridges.
supportExplanation: The final Atlantic City paragraph gives the Pontiac and Pennsylvania locations, while the contemporary AP dispatch records the authorities’ earlier confidence in the cordon.
qualification: The summary traces the fugitives beyond Atlantic City and leaves their exit route and any clothing-store visit open. The records give no chronology for the bridge patrols relative to the escape.

assertion: A federal prosecutor said Segar obtained two types of keys in Denver and recruited an alleged mail-theft crew in Saint Paul.
locators: S147, Printed p. 1, ‘Bare Conspiracy To Rob U.S. Mail And Peddle Loot,’ last paragraph before the jump. | S148, Printed p. 5, continuation headed ‘Bare Conspiracy,’ opening paragraph.
supportExplanation: The front-page dispatch names Segar and the two sets of keys. The continuation says he returned to Saint Paul and names two alleged recruits.
qualification: This is the prosecutor’s description of the alleged scheme as reported in 1936. The dispatch gives no account of how Segar obtained the keys.

assertion: The prosecutor described a pattern of opening station mailrooms and sacks, taking the registered mail, and locking both again before leaving.
locators: S148, Printed p. 5, ‘Bare Conspiracy,’ quoted paragraphs beginning ‘In many small towns’ and describing relocking the sacks and building.
supportExplanation: The page 5 continuation specifies where mail was left overnight and what the prosecutor said the two key sets opened.
qualification: The newspaper quotes the prosecutor describing an alleged recurring method. This passage gives no list of the stations or a count for individual trips.

assertion: The May 1936 dispatch reports eleven arrests in an alleged mail-theft conspiracy and attributes the $100 Liberty bond lead to the prosecutor.
locators: S147, Printed p. 1, May 9 Denver dateline, list of arrests and paragraph beginning ‘A $100 liberty bond.’
supportExplanation: The front-page dispatch gives the number under arrest, names the two men held in Saint Paul and connects the Liberty bond to the investigation.
qualification: The dispatch names people under arrest and gives the prosecution’s account. The outcome of the case remains unverified.
